#10029. Now on Amazon CloudWatch Omni: collaborative AI-powered observability for your applications

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Amazon CloudWatch now offers CloudWatch Omni, an AI-powered observability experience for the applications and AI agents you run together. You reach Omni through a dedicated URL for your organization and sign in with the identities you already manage, so working in Omni does not require access to the AWS Management Console. Omni is built on OpenTelemetry: the telemetry you already send to CloudWatch appears in Omni with nothing to reconfigure, and any other workload you instrument with OpenTelemetry sends its telemetry to an OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) endpoint.

CloudWatch Omni offers both agent observability and application observability in a single experience. In our companion post, we introduced the agent observability capabilities of Omni for generative AI and agentic workloads. In this post, we present the application observability experience.

Engineering teams spend a significant portion of their observability time maintaining dashboards, tuning thresholds, and switching between tools to piece together what happened during an incident. When an issue crosses team boundaries, context gets lost in Slack threads and screenshots rather than flowing naturally to the next engineer. CloudWatch Omni changes this by organizing observability around your applications rather than individual signals, and bringing your whole team into the same workspace.

What CloudWatch Omni brings CloudWatch Omni addresses three problems that engineering teams told us they face today.

One collaborative experience for your whole team. Every engineer accesses CloudWatch Omni through a single URL with enterprise SSO (via IAM Identity Center, supporting Okta, EntraID, and other providers). No AWS Console access is required. SREs, developers, database engineers, and managers share the same data and investigation context. When an investigation escalates, the next person joins the same session with full context already in front of them.

The system adapts as your applications evolve. CloudWatch Omni discovers your services, maps dependencies, and adjusts alarms automatically. Instead of manually curating dashboards and tuning thresholds, you declare what matters (availability targets, latency budgets, error rate thresholds) and Omni adapts as your system changes. When you deploy new services, Omni updates the application topology automatically.

AI-powered investigation with Amazon DevOps Agent. Amazon DevOps Agent participates alongside your team in investigation sessions, correlating signals and suggesting next steps. The agent works from the same telemetry your engineers see, so its suggestions are grounded in the actual state of your application. It identifies correlated events across services, traces root cause paths through your dependency graph, and maintains investigation history for post-incident review.

How an investigation works When something breaks, CloudWatch Omni opens an investigation session pre-loaded with context. Here is a typical incident workflow:

An alarm fires on elevated error rates in your checkout service. Omni opens a session showing the service topology, correlated signals (a deployment 10 minutes earlier, increased latency from a downstream payment API), and DevOps Agent’s initial analysis.

Your on-call SRE confirms the deployment correlation, pulls in the trace view to identify failing endpoints, and checks if the payment API latency correlates with a capacity limit.

The SRE escalates to the payments team. The payments engineer joins the same session and sees everything found so far, plus DevOps Agent’s correlation with a configuration change in the payment provider’s API gateway. They identify the root cause and roll back.

The entire investigation history is captured automatically. No separate incident report needed.

Walkthrough: setting up your first Space To set up CloudWatch Omni for your team, open the CloudWatch console and click “Try CloudWatch Omni.”

Next, connect your identity provider through IAM Identity Center (supporting Okta, Azure AD, and other SAML 2.0 providers). Once connected, your team members access Omni directly at your dedicated URL without needing AWS Console credentials.

Create a Space for your team. A Space groups the applications your team owns and the telemetry associated with them.

Once created, Omni discovers your services automatically and maps the dependencies between them. You see your application topology immediately.

You can ask CloudWatch Omni any question about your applications in plain English, and Omni will analyze your telemetry data and surface insights.

You can also set up service health alerts, configure what matters to your team, and trigger an AWS DevOps agent investigation to identify the root cause and develop a mitigation plan.

Application-centric organization CloudWatch Omni organizes telemetry by application rather than by infrastructure component. The system automatically discovers services from the telemetry data and AWS Config resource discovery, maps dependencies, and lets you see your application as a connected system rather than a collection of isolated resources.

Each team gets a Space that contains the applications they own. A Space points at existing CloudWatch data (logs, metrics, traces, and alarms) with no additional data movement required. Dynamic views replace the maintenance burden of static dashboards, providing ongoing visibility into SLOs and application health.

Getting started Getting started takes minutes and doesn’t require reconfiguration of your existing CloudWatch setup.

If you’re an existing CloudWatch customer: Click “Try CloudWatch Omni” in the CloudWatch console. All your existing telemetry (logs, metrics, traces, and alarms) is immediately available. Workloads are discovered automatically, and you can start an investigation or browse your application topology right away.

For organization-wide deployment: An administrator configures a domain, connects your identity provider via IAM Identity Center, defines Spaces for teams and environments, and invites users. Each Space points at existing CloudWatch data with no additional data movement required.

For applications in other environments: CloudWatch Omni provides connectors that make it easy to bring in telemetry from additional environments. All ingested telemetry appears alongside your AWS data in the same Spaces and investigation sessions.

For generative AI and agentic workloads: The same CloudWatch Omni experience delivers purpose-built observability for AI agents, including trace exploration, evaluation frameworks, and real-time monitoring. In our companion post, we introduced the agent observability capabilities of Omni; for that walkthrough, see Introducing Amazon CloudWatch Omni: AI-powered observability for generative AI and agentic workloads.

Pricing and availability Amazon CloudWatch Omni is now available. Existing CloudWatch customers can try it directly from the CloudWatch console. For pricing details, visit the Amazon CloudWatch pricing page.

To get started, visit Amazon CloudWatch Omni or click “Try CloudWatch Omni” in the Amazon CloudWatch console.

#10026. Introducing enhanced custom event buses in Amazon EventBridge for enterprise-scale event-driven applications

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Organizations building event-driven applications on Amazon EventBridge typically start with a single custom event bus in one account. This works well when a single team owns the architecture. As adoption grows across the organization, though, things get complicated. AWS best practices recommend a multi-account structure, which means each team runs in its own account. To route events between them, teams create multiple event buses connected through cross-account rules or bus-to-bus configurations. This workaround reintroduces the operational complexity that serverless architectures are meant to eliminate. Platform teams lose visibility into who is subscribing to which events, cross-account and bus-to-bus routing charges compound quickly, and teams that need capabilities like event ordering are forced to build complex workarounds or adopt entirely different technologies.

The Create custom event bus page. Custom event bus is the recommended new option, with ordered delivery, filter patterns, event replay, and sharing across your AWS organization. Custom event bus – classic remains available for existing workloads.

Next, I configured resource sharing. I turned on Enable event bus sharing and selected Allow sharing only within your organization. I chose AWS account ID as the principal type. I could also share with an organization, an organizational unit, or an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role or user. Sharing uses AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM), so I did not have to set up cross-account permissions or bus-to-bus routing myself.

Event orderingEvent-driven architectures work best when consumers are designed around asynchronous patterns, where the order of events does not matter. There are a few cases where order does matter. In a logistics application, driver location updates must arrive in sequence. Out-of-sequence events cause routing algorithms to make decisions based on stale data.

To support ordered processing, the enhanced custom event bus includes synchronous invocation for targets like AWS Lambda. Synchronous mode confirms successful processing before acknowledging the event, eliminating the common pattern of placing Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) between an event bus and Lambda to ensure reliability.

Event evaluationPublishers can turn on content-based deduplication so EventBridge detects and drops retries of the same event from the payload itself. You do not have to generate and track a deduplication ID when a timeout or a partial failure sends the same event twice. EventBridge hashes the meaningful parts of the event and collapses matches that arrive within five minutes, which gives those retries exactly-once delivery semantics instead of EventBridge’s usual at-least-once model. If you already stamp your own idempotency token, keep using it. Content-based deduplication is for sources that cannot reliably identify the same event on a retry.

Existing EventBridge custom event buses continue to work as they do today with no changes required. They now appear as Custom event bus – classic. The enhanced custom event bus is a new resource that you adopt at your own pace. In the console, it appears as Custom event bus.

Now availableThe enhanced custom event bus is available today in the US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland, Frankfurt, Stockholm, Spain), and Asia Pacific (Hong Kong, Malaysia, Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Thailand, Tokyo) Regions. You can create your first enhanced custom event bus through the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or EventBridge APIs. To get started, visit the EventBridge documentation or try it out directly in the EventBridge console.

#10025. GSMA warns of growing risks to mobile networks from extreme weather

Mobile comms body wants a joined-up approach from governments and regulators to mitigate downtime

The GSMA wants governments and regulators to work more closely with mobile operators to help protect networks against growing risks from extreme weather.

As the global body representing the mobile network industry, the GSMA claims that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion annually to repair damage to cell radio sites, and it believes that figure could nearly double to more than $3 billion a year by 2050, under the climate conditions expected then.

The GSMA sets out its findings in a six-part research series, Futureproofing Connectivity: Climate Risk and Resilience in Telecommunications, alongside a separate document outlining its Policy Principles for Mobile Network Resilience.

The report identifies weather-related risks that can affect telecoms networks, along with the associated restoration costs. Towers, masts, and rooftop sites are particularly exposed to wind and storms or lightning, for example, while ground-level equipment at mobile sites can be inundated in flooding incidents.

High temperatures can cause radio equipment to overheat, while heavy rain can degrade wireless signal strength, and infrastructure in coastal locations may be exposed to storm surges.

However, the report fingers the electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability. If that gets knocked out, the network could go offline once any backup power is exhausted, which may take anywhere from a few hours to considerably longer, depending on the site.

Under current climate conditions, the cost of damage to cell sites is estimated at $1 billion associated with severe storms, while river and coastal floods account for $577 million and $124 million, respectively.

Based on projected mid-century climate conditions, the GSMA expects costs due to severe storms to rise significantly to about $2.37 billion, accounting for three-quarters of all damage.

The report asserts that cell network resilience requires a whole ecosystem approach, pointing out that if severe weather impacts power networks, then that also affects the telecoms infrastructure.

The GSMA says that network firms have traditionally managed the operational risks that may affect network availability, but claims they face barriers in conducting full assessments of those associated with climate change.

Some of these barriers are internal, such as lack of shared information between departments. Other barriers are in the different regulatory reporting frameworks, with infrastructure rules tending to focus on service continuity, while climate disclosure frameworks focus on governance, financial exposure, and reporting for investors and other stakeholders.

The report lists separate recommendations for network firms and for policymakers and regulators.

Operators are advised to embed resilience by design, using modeled projections for severe weather and future risk scenarios. They are also told to plan and test resilience across the wider ecosystem, engaging with others such as public authorities.

When it comes to policymakers and regulators, the report asks for resilience frameworks to be developed through consultation with the operators. It also advises coordination among mobile operators, electricity and fuel providers, and emergency services to help maintain vital communications during major disruptions.

And as if that isn't enough to chew over, the separate policy document sets out five principles for governments and regulators. These include avoiding prescriptive regulations and instead promoting outcome-based policies, encouraging dialog and consultation between governments, regulators, and operators, and developing resilience as a cross-sector responsibility.

“Mobile connectivity is essential infrastructure,” says GSMA Foundation president and chief regulatory officer John Giusti.

“Whether responding to extreme weather, power failures or other major disruptions, people, businesses and emergency services depend heavily on mobile networks,” he added.

“Severe weather is already costing the industry billions of dollars, and those costs are set to rise substantially. Building resilience will require a coordinated effort amongst operators, governments and the wider ecosystem.” ®

#10022. Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services

LiteRT in Google Play services is Android's on-device inference runtime for custom models, handling more than a trillion inferences a day across billions of devices. Today, it gets its biggest upgrade yet: GPU inference that runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy GPU delegate, powered by ML Drift and available through the new CompiledModel API, LiteRT’s modern successor to the legacy Interpreter API.

Until now, taking advantage of this faster GPU stack required bundling LiteRT in your app. In our testing, apps that switched to LiteRT in Google Play services are about 8 MB smaller, making them faster to download and lighter on users' devices, because the runtime, including the GPU accelerator, ships once with Play services rather than inside every app. More than 100K Android apps bundle their own copy of LiteRT or TensorFlow Lite today, so the savings add up quickly as apps switch.

If your Android app runs custom ML models on CPU or GPU, we encourage you to switch to LiteRT in Google Play services. You can see it in action in the Google AI Edge Gallery app, where the Scrapbook feature's image segmentation runs on LiteRT in Google Play services.

Developers that adopt LiteRT in Google Play Services enjoy immediate benefits:

LiteRT is the evolution of TensorFlow Lite. It keeps the same .tflite model format you rely on and adds the CompiledModel API, which makes acceleration across fragmented hardware reliable:

Whether you're starting fresh or switching from bundled LiteRT, using LiteRT in Google Play services takes a few lines of code:

If you're already using the legacy Interpreter API in Google Play services, your Interpreter code keeps working on CPU when you switch to play-services-litert. To run on the GPU, move to the CompiledModel API.

Let your coding agent do the work. In Agent Mode, the new LiteRT skill for Android Studio automates the move to LiteRT in Google Play services and the CompiledModel API. Ask it to “migrate my TFLite code to CompiledModel,” or type @litert-runtime, and it switches your app to play-services-litert, rewrites your Interpreter calls, and sets up GPU acceleration with CPU fallback. It can also scaffold a new LiteRT app. Treat it as a strong first pass: review the diff, build, and compare outputs on a real device. Get the skill on GitHub.

Upgrading from legacy APIs? The legacy GPU delegate and custom delegate APIs are deprecated in favor of CompiledModel GPU acceleration and the Compiler Plugin and Dispatch APIs, and NNAPI will be removed starting in 2027. Older SDKs now receive critical security fixes only. Apps you've already shipped keep working, but plan your move to the CompiledModel API now: code that uses deprecated APIs won't compile against the latest SDK, and staying on an older SDK can cause conflicts as your other dependencies move forward. See the release notes for details.

Looking ahead, LiteRT in Google Play services is our foundation for running your own task-specific models on Android, with CPU and GPU acceleration.

#10018. AI policy wonks declare 'sovereign agents' a threat to civilization

These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and 'pursue open-ended, evolving survival'

The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves.

These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.”

Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote.

A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for  ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve.

AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack.

“If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.”

There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report.

First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting.

The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. And it suggests a public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group - formed in 2009 to combat the Conficker worm - to boost chokepoints against  sovereign agents before they emerge.

Other policy recommendations suggest lawmakers enforce human verification and cybersecurity standards for services that the working group identifies as essential to sovereign agents, and calls on departments of State, Treasury, Justice, and Homeland Security to disrupt any gray-market access to unauthorized services.

Finally, “Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow,” the report recommends.

This hits on something your humble Reg vultures have been hissing about for quite some time now – and would likely solve all future incidents involving rogue, or sovereign, AI agents: hold frontier labs’ human bosses legally liable for their agents' illegal actions.  ®

All of this has happened before. All of this will happen again. Maybe

#10014. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL now supports direct querying of Apache Iceberg and Parquet data in your data lake

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing a new capability for Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL that you can use to directly query operational data together with data stored in your data lake in Apache Iceberg and Apache Parquet formats, using your existing PostgreSQL applications and tools. By eliminating the need to extract, transform, and load (ETL) structured data from data lakes into your operational database, you can reduce operational complexity and simplify application development. You can also use Aurora PostgreSQL to query data from data lakes managed in Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC)-compatible catalogs, giving you access to data across a breadth of analytics systems without moving or duplicating it. Whether you’re powering real-time dashboards, enriching transactions with historical context, or building AI agents that reason over both live and archived data, you can now do it all through a single, familiar interface.

Previously, if your application needed to combine recent transactional data in Aurora with historical records stored in Amazon S3, a common approach was to build reverse ETL pipelines that duplicated data, increased infrastructure costs, and required ongoing engineering effort to keep everything synchronized. This challenge only grows as you increasingly embed AI agents into your applications, where it is impractical to predict and pre-replicate every dataset an agent might need.

DuckLabs, the team that maintains the DuckDB project, recently joined Amazon, and this capability is an example of how the efficiency of DuckDB is being integrated into our services. DuckDB is now embedded directly within Aurora PostgreSQL, so you can query live operational data (including uncommitted writes) alongside your data lake in a single query. Query processing stays within Aurora, with no additional network hops and no ETL pipelines that duplicate data. You can query Apache Iceberg tables managed through the AWS Glue Data Catalog, as well as Parquet and Iceberg data stored in Amazon S3 and S3 Tables. You do all of this using familiar PostgreSQL syntax and your existing applications and tools.

We’re excited to bring the speed and simplicity of DuckDB directly into Aurora PostgreSQL, so you and your agents can query and combine operational and Iceberg data using the familiar PostgreSQL applications, tools, and endpoints already in use. By building this capability around DuckDB, future improvements to the open source engine can continue to bring performance and functionality gains to Aurora and other AWS services.

What is newThis capability is supported on two Aurora PostgreSQL major versions: 17 (starting with 17.11) and 18 (starting with 18.6). To use it, you create an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster, attach an IAM role with the AuroraAnalytics feature, and enable the aurora_analytics extension. The IAM role is what gives Aurora access to your data in Amazon S3 and the AWS Glue Data Catalog. You then create foreign tables that point to your Iceberg or Parquet data in the data lake, and query them using familiar PostgreSQL syntax. You can complete this setup through the Amazon RDS console, or with any PostgreSQL client such as psql. The process is well documented in the Aurora PostgreSQL documentation.

You can query data across external IRC-compatible catalogs through AWS Glue Data Catalog federation. You register the external catalog once with Glue, and then create foreign tables for the tables you want to query, the same way you would for any Glue-native table. A single query can then join data stored in Aurora with Iceberg tables registered across multiple catalogs, so applications get a unified view without moving data or replacing your existing catalog investments.

Aurora also applies optimizations such as predicate pushdown and column pruning so that only the relevant data is read. This keeps queries efficient even as the underlying data grows. Frequently accessed data is also cached in your Aurora instance, so subsequent queries against the same data return faster. You can inspect this behavior per query using aurora_analytics_stat_statements(), which reports metrics such as rows scanned, bytes read from Amazon S3, and cache hits.

To see how direct querying works, I connected to my Aurora PostgreSQL database using psql and created the extension:

For my walkthrough, I set up a simple financial scenario. I have a recent_transactions table in Aurora with the last 7 days of customer transactions, and a Parquet file in Amazon S3 containing 5 years of historical transaction data. To make Aurora aware of the historical data, I created a foreign table pointing at the Parquet file in S3:

Notice the empty parentheses in the CREATE FOREIGN TABLE statement. Aurora automatically reads the schema from the Parquet file metadata, so you do not need to define columns manually. For workloads with many tables, you can skip creating them one at a time: a single IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA statement bulk-creates foreign tables for every Iceberg or Parquet table in an AWS Glue Data Catalog database, inferring schemas automatically.

With both tables in place, I ran a single query that combines the recent operational data in Aurora with the historical data in S3:

The result shows both recent and historical transactions in a single result set. The 7 most recent rows come from Aurora, and the rest come directly from the Parquet file in S3. DuckDB handles the analytical scan of the Parquet data under the hood, while Aurora handles the operational data. That single query would have previously required a pipeline to move the historical data into the database first.

If a query pattern needs single-digit-millisecond latency, you can materialize data from the data lake into a native Aurora PostgreSQL table using familiar commands such as CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, INSERT INTO ... SELECT, or MERGE INTO. The materialized table lives in Aurora and is queried like any other PostgreSQL table, giving you a low-latency path for hot data without operating a separate ingestion pipeline. The read queries can run on any Aurora PostgreSQL instance in your cluster, whether the writer or a read replica, so you can offload analytical scans from your operational workload. The materialization commands write data into Aurora, so they run on the writer instance.

Get started today Direct querying of Apache Iceberg and Parquet data from Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL is available today in all commercial AWS Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, at no additional charge. You pay only for the incremental Aurora compute the queries consume and Amazon S3 request costs for reading data lake files.

To learn more, visit the Amazon Aurora features page, read the Aurora PostgreSQL documentation, or try it in the Amazon RDS console. We welcome your feedback through AWS re:Post or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Esra Kayabali is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, specializing in analytics, including data warehousing, data lakes, big data analytics, batch and real-time data streaming, and data integration. She has more than ten years of software development and solution architecture experience. She is passionate about collaborative learning, knowledge sharing, and guiding community in their cloud technologies journey.

#10013. British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted

Turns out cheap tokens get engineers doing things that save time, like debugging and tackling Jira tickets

Revolut says that in less than a year it's managed to slash its AI coding inference costs by roughly 90 percent by making self-hosted models its default instead of relying primarily on commercial services like Claude.

Speaking at the AI Engineer conference in New York last month, David Abitbol, ops and infrastructure lead at the British fintech, described how it saw a 60 percent improvement in coding time and a 70 percent improvement in lead time following its rollout of AI coding tools to roughly 2,000 engineers. Revolut initially adopted GLM-5.1 before moving to GLM-5.3, which it now serves using 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs.

Prior to its switch to GLM, Revolut had been experimenting with AI, deploying Gemini in early 2025 and Claude Code in early 2026. "We were highly skeptical about the cost of AI. We were seeing engineers spend $1,000 a month, $10,000 a month with not so much ROI, and so when we launched it we launched it with strict budget limits," Abitbol said.

Because of this, engineers only had access to a limited number of tokens, so the company began investigating self-hosting its own models. At $0.30 per million input/output tokens, self hosting GLM 5.1 cost about a tenth of using OpenAI's Codex or Anthropic's Claude Code. And, as it turned out, when tokens are cheap, you stop worrying about how many they use or what they use them for.

While Revolut did see improvements to coding speed, Abitbol noted the biggest bottleneck wasn't actually the code. Instead, he says the biggest gains came from letting the AI models deal with things like debugging and Jira and Confluence tickets. "When you have unlimited tokens, you're free to do that," he said. "You no longer have to save your tokens for the end of the quarter or the most difficult task."

Developed by Chinese open weights model dev Z.ai, GLM 5.1 isn't exactly a small model. At roughly 754 billion total parameters (40 billion activated for each token generated), the model requires roughly 380 GB of GPU memory just to hold the weights and another 6-26 GB per user to maintain context depending on precision.

To serve GLM-5.3 at scale, Revolut deployed 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs, equivalent in GPU count to seven eight-GPU DGX B200 systems. But as Abitbol noted, the greatest performance gains didn't come from adding GPUs, but rather tuning the model's hyperparameters along with switching to NVFP4 quantization, implementing disaggregated prefill and decode, and tuning context lengths.

One key takeaway was that supporting a one-million-token context window doesn't necessarily make such a large window useful or efficient. "Long context is a scam. You really need to be mindful of that," Abitbol said. "Even though you can serve one million tokens, 256 [thousand] is really what you need."

With these optimizations, Abitbol says that the company was able to achieve sub 3-second time to first token on context windows of around 256,000 tokens, and generation speeds of around 200 tokens a second, both of which he notes are the sweet spot for the company's software engineers.

"What you want to aim for is a sub-3 second time to first token. This is empirical evidence. As soon as you exceed 5 seconds, my Slack inbox starts to blow up," Abitbol said. "In terms of throughput, it doesn't really matter as much. We serve, in terms of interactivity, 200 tokens per second. People are fine [with that]. You don't need to go higher. The way people work has changed. We no longer look at the stream of thinking tokens. People run tasks in parallel and check in when the task is done."

And if throughput is a concern, he notes engineers who sign in after 5 pm are getting closer to 800 tokens a second.

However, it's worth noting that GLM hasn't replaced GPT or Claude entirely. The Chinese model is text only, so it isn't ideal for things like UI work. So instead, Revolut used a model router to direct vision queries to models like Gemini or GPT Luna while keeping code generation running on GLM.

"Open source is now a priority at Revolut, and our economics are favorable. The billing is flat, we don't have any bill shock at the end of the month, and the frontier is the exception," Abitbol said.

#10011. Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Threat actors don't need to rely on malware to breach organizations anymore. They're simply calling help desks and politely asking for access, with a little help from artificial intelligence.

After a disruptive cyberattack hits, customer trust can take a while to rebuild. But now threat actors are impersonating trusted brand names and existing customer accounts to abuse customer relations.

"Trust has become easier to exploit and harder to establish," a new TransUnion report warns. Threat actors use social engineering, deepfake technology, text spoofing, compromised credentials, and artificial intelligence (AI) to become whoever they need to be, whether that's a new or existing customer or the organization itself.

In light of more attacks, many organizations have improved security during sign-up and onboarding processes. Organizations must continue to adapt since "most fraud now occurs after the customer relationship has already been established," the report states. It found 58% of organizations were very or extremely concerned that fraud is evolving faster than their abilities to detect or prevent it.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

The use of synthetic identities plays a big role. Threat actors can spin them up with ease, given widespread data breaches that exposed millions of individuals' sensitive information, says Brian Killeen, vice president of global identity solutions at TransUnion. Scammers will replicate leaked documents or use deepfakes to bypass identity proofing checks at onboarding.

The credit reporting agency found that account login accounted for 53% of all suspected digital fraud during the first half of 2026. Conducting scams has become easier for threat actors as tooling advances, Killeen adds. Threat actors aren't just automating account creation with scripts; they're actually building logic into automated pipelines to reverse-engineer security controls, he says. That allows them to pinpoint exactly where and how defenses are blocking their attacks.

"Trust is under pressure," Killeen tells Dark Reading.

Last year the FBI warned of an uptick in cybercriminals targeting employee self-service portals — websites used for payroll, benefits, and other human resources services — at both private companies and government agencies. Threat actors created fake search engine advertisements to lure users into visiting malicious sites that mimicked legitimate companies' logos and layouts. Once the victim logged in, attackers stole login credentials and financial information.

And the situation continues to evolve. Over the past year, AI has helped criminals personalize attacks and spread them across channels — from email to Teams. Deepfakes add another layer of credibility, says Javvad Malik, lead chief information security officer (CISO) adviser at KnowBe4.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Amid booming AI adoption that security has trouble matching, the security awareness company is also seeing more attempts to exploit AI systems or take advantage of poorly configured AI tools and agents, he adds.

"The social engineering techniques remain similar, but attackers are also using AI to find weaknesses and are beginning to target AI agents directly," Malik tells Dark Reading.

The AI attack surface is ripe for the taking. New research from Check Point on brand impersonation trends from Q3 flagged a phishing campaign where threat actors impersonated Anthropic's Claude assistant. Fraudulent emails, playing up urgency with a due payment notice, requested 500 euros with an "update payment" link intended to trick users into clicking, putting their credentials and financial information at risk. Since April, KnowBe4 tracked a 228% increase in AI brand impersonation, says James Dyer, head of threat intelligence. Attackers are abusing the global focus on using AI within businesses as a perfect covert operation for their phishing attacks, he adds, warning that the problem compounds when attackers center their attacks around breaking news headlines.

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

When it comes to attacks against customer relations, attackers' methods have evolved from deploying malware to exploiting identity because there's no need to write a script when they can just get a password reset, says Dave Lewis, global advisory CISO at 1Password.

The industry spent a decade training people not to click links, and attackers responded by simply asking nicely, he adds. The most common attacks he has observed don't involve "anyone in a hoodie typing furiously" but instead phoning the help desk to manipulate users into giving away multifactor authentication (MFA) codes.

"[It's] the most effective zero-day of 2026," Lewis says.

Walking in through the customer relationship management (CRM) system's front door is another tactic he has seen, pointing to the data-theft campaign against Salesforce customers that started in 2025 and continued into 2026.

"Nobody 'hacks' the CRM," Lewis tells Dark Reading. "They just log in with a key you handed to a vendor or a guest account nobody remembers creating."

The target moved from the data center to the software-as-a-service layer, where one compromised integration gives attackers many targets per compromise. Detection lags because SaaS platforms log differently from traditional infrastructure, Lewis adds.

Threat actors also use AI to build voice deepfakes from executives' public recordings, deploy them in high-pressure desk calls, and then use AI again to move through hybrid environments within minutes of gaining access. But that doesn't exactly signal an increase in sophistication, Lewis says.

"Technical sophistication is down," he says. "Operational sophistication — research, patience, scripting, follow-through — is up. It's less of the 'evil genius' and more 'well-run call center with bad intentions.'"

"What once looked legitimate and trusted can change" as threat actors slip further under the radar, cloaked behind more convincing and personalized impersonation tactics. Killeen stresses. Organizations across industries are seeing more scams, authorized fraud, and good customers being manipulated, he says.

Organizations must learn and adapt quickly because attackers aren't wasting any time. Killeen recommends that organizations take a look at their existing controls to uncover vulnerable points and understand where the biggest losses are. Even if organizations stand up strong security at the front door, they could still fall victim to downstream risks.

"It's taking a risk-based approach, looking at things holistically, and how you prioritize those things accordingly, based on your vulnerabilities," Killeen advises.

Killeen and Lewis agree that attacks against customer relations warrants checking every door leading into the CRM. That includes every OAuth application, integration, guest or portal user, and API key.

"Revoke anything without a named owner," Lewis says. "Scope the rest. Repeat quarterly because they grow back."

He also recommends that organizations fix the help desk process attackers continually abuse, rather than people who work it. Scripted identity verification for resets, callback to a number of record, and manager approval for any privileged or MFA reset are ways to reduce risk in that area.

"Drop speed metrics, like average handle time, for identity-sensitive support interactions," Lewis adds. “They drive agents to prioritize speed over verification.”

Holding less customer data is another area organizations can prioritize to limit risks. Implement retention limits on customer records, purge dormant accounts, and don't include production customer data in sandboxes, Lewis recommends.

"Data you don't hold can't be stolen," he says.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#10010. Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents

Agent-User Interactions are now evolving from text exchanges to rich UIs. Until recently, most conversations looked like this:

User: "Find me a holiday package to Bali in March." Agent: (six packages in prose, each with dates, hotel, flights, price) User: "The five-night one with breakfast." Agent: "Here's the link. You can book it on the operator's site."

Agents could plan the trip, but everything came back as walls of text. They had no standard way to render a selectable list of packages, a map of the destinations, or a date picker to carry you through the rest of the booking, inside the conversation itself.

Generative UI is the layer that lets agents build interfaces at runtime, shaped by what each request needs - giving users a rich, interactive experience. Implementing that takes two pieces: a way to describe the UI and an agentic stack that connects your agent to your application and renders that UI.

Generative UI covers a spectrum of approaches, from using predefined higher order components, to enabling your AI agent to have the flexibility to decide how to build the UI.

At the controlled end, you build each component ahead of time, and the agent picks which one to render and with what data. It's brand-safe but it does not allow for deep customization and personalization based on the user’s intent. At the open end, the agent returns a raw UI program written in HTML, Javascript and/or Dart that renders inside a sandboxed iframe. That covers anything you did not plan for, at the cost of a surface that drifts from your design system and executes code a model wrote.

A2UI works through the entire spectrum. It participates in controlled generation with decision models like Typesafe’s Jev and also open-ended code generation that may output A2UI JSON messages. The declarative mode, where agents assemble pre-declared components and functions, is the most popular. A2UI is the framework-agnostic standard for declaring UI intent, so local or remote agents can generate your UI from your existing component catalog using a common language.

Frontend developers can now ship the building blocks once, and the agent composes them for each request.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

The Basic Catalog ships 18 general-purpose primitives across layout, display, input, and containers. The agent can compose entirely different interfaces from the same 18 primitives, depending on what the request needs.

The Basic Catalog is deliberately sparse, so most production apps define their own custom catalog. A custom component can be anything your frontend already renders, including a live map the agent fills with coordinates while your renderer draws the route.

CopilotKit is built on AG-UI (Agent-User Interaction Protocol), which supports A2UI payload and provides Agent SDKs across many agentic backends.

Your agent emits A2UI operations. AG-UI carries them to the client as typed events. When the user takes any action, the values are sent back along the same stream.

A2UI works with any AG-UI compatible agent. Frameworks like Google ADK, LangChain, Mastra and Strands are all AG-UI compatible, so the setup is identical whichever one your agent runs on.

Setup comes down to two things: connecting your agent to CopilotKit, and defining which components the agent is allowed to use.

Using Google ADK as the example, the ag_ui_adk package wraps any ADK agent and serves it as an AG-UI endpoint on FastAPI:

On the app side, you register that endpoint with the CopilotKit runtime at /api/copilotkit. It's a few lines of standard setup, covered in the Google ADK quickstart, and it needs nothing A2UI-specific.

A2UI itself turns on from the client, where your components already are. Define what the agent is allowed to draw, map each definition to a renderer, and pass the catalog to the CopilotKit provider.

The description goes into the agent's prompt, so the model knows when to reach for FlightCard instead of a generic card. The Zod schema validates the props it sends back.

The A2UI configuration can be set up ahead of time on the server, or it can be created dynamically, shipped from the client to the server with the request. The ADK code above used dynamic configuration which is why it used generate_a2ui without defining it. The docs cover both approaches.

That’s the CopilotKit path. You can also consume the event stream directly with @ag-ui/client and hand the A2UI operations to any compliant renderer: @a2ui/react, or the Flutter, Lit, or Angular equivalent.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Most agent-generated UI is one-shot. The agent draws something, you read it, and it goes stale the moment anything changes.

A2UI surfaces are bi-directional and the components are reactive, which makes multi-step flows possible. Any action the user takes on the interface (picking dates, choosing a flight, entering passenger details) travels back along the same stream, and the agent re-emits the surface from there using those values.

Here is a high-level architecture example of an end-to-end booking flow, with an AG-UI agent on Cloud Run streaming A2UI surfaces to a CopilotKit frontend.

Two things make the round trip work: inputs bound to a data path, and a button carrying an action that names which paths to send back.

Validation runs on the client, so a bad email shows an error inline without a model call. Nothing reaches the agent until the button fires.

Then the client sends the bound values, and the agent re-emits against the same surfaceId. That is how the whole flow lives on one surface: flight search, results, passenger details, and confirmation.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Every AG-UI integration inherets these benefits, so you don't have to build them yourself:

Create a complete A2UI + CopilotKit application. This creates a starter A2UI application with Copilotkit Agent integration.

The CopilotKit Dojo has runnable A2UI demos: fixed server-side schema, dynamic schema against a custom catalog, and an error-recovery example where an invalid first render heals into a valid one.

Explore how to build Generative UI Agents with CopilotKit, or dive into A2UI documentation to learn how to integrate A2UI with any framework of your choice.

#10009. Amazon S3 Vectors now supports metadata pre-filtering for higher recall on filtered searches

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing metadata pre-filtering for Amazon S3 Vectors, which delivers higher recall on filtered queries by evaluating your metadata filter before the similarity search. You can filter on attributes such as tenant, category, status, or time, and pre-filtering adds prefix matching with $startsWith for paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. Each vector carries up to 2 KB of filterable metadata, and a single query supports up to 100 filter constraints. There is no additional cost, no re-ingestion, and no change to your queries.

Most applications never search a whole index. They search the part of it that belongs to a particular user, account, or category, and they express that scope as a metadata filter. Semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic applications all need the same thing from a filtered query: a similarity search that covers the vectors matching the filter, and returns the closest of them. With pre-filtering, a filtered query returns more of the relevant matches your index contains, giving you higher recall on filtered searches.

Common use cases Pre-filtering applies wherever results have to be both relevant and correctly scoped:

How pre-filtering works Each vector in an S3 Vectors index can carry application-defined metadata, and a query can filter on those fields.

Every vector index has an index mode. On an index whose index mode is ENHANCED, S3 Vectors resolves your filter first, then searches only the vectors that match. On an index whose index mode is CLASSIC, S3 Vectors performs the vector search and filter evaluation in tandem, validating each candidate vector against your filter as it searches. Existing indexes use CLASSIC until you update them.

Consider a support knowledge base of 8 million tickets, where an agent searches one customer’s history for a recurring error. If that customer accounts for 400 of those tickets, resolving customer_id first means the similarity search runs across all 400 of them, so the agent sees that customer’s prior occurrences. Before the index was updated, the same query drew its candidates from the full 8 million, and the result set contained fewer of that customer’s matching tickets.

On highly selective filters, pre-filtering returns up to 5x more of the matching vectors than the same query returned before on CLASSIC indexes.

Getting started Before you start, make sure your IAM policy grants permissions for the new actions.

You can get started in three steps. The walkthrough below builds a small product-catalog index and runs a selective filter against it, the same pattern you would use for a multi-tenant RAG store or a document search scoped to one client.

The dimension must match the output size of your embedding model, and distance-metric should match how that model was trained (cosine is common for text embeddings). Second, write vectors with the PutVectors API, attaching up to 2 KB of filterable metadata to each vector:

Each vector carries the attributes your application filters on. In this example, tenant_id scopes results to a single customer, category narrows by document type, created_date records when the document was created, and active is a boolean flag. By default every metadata field is filterable, so you can query on any of them without declaring a schema up front.

Third, run a filtered similarity query with the QueryVectors API. The filter uses a compact JSON syntax where a bare key-value pair is an equality match, and operators such as $and, $or, and $gt combine or refine conditions. Pass --return-metadata so the query returns each vector’s metadata:

The expected result is a single vector, doc-001, the only one matching all three filter conditions (tenant_id, category, and active):

S3 Vectors first narrows the search space to vectors matching all three filter conditions, then returns the 50 most similar vectors from that subset. Because the filter is applied before the search, those results are drawn from across all the vectors that match it.

Prefix matching with $startsWith Pre-filtering adds a prefix match operator for filtering on paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. A document store that encodes case and folder structure into a document ID can scope a search to a subtree in one condition:

$startsWith joins the existing operators: equality, numeric range, set membership, existence checks, and boolean logic with $and and $or.

Turning on pre-filtering for existing indexes Call UpdateIndexMode on an existing index to turn on pre-filtering:

Pre-filtering takes effect in place. Your existing vectors are not re-ingested, your queries do not change, and the new filter operators are available immediately.

Here is the difference on the same index and the same query. Before the update, a query scoped to one tenant returns two of the ten results requested:

After the update, the same query returns a full result set drawn from across that tenant’s documents:

Rolling out across your indexes Once you have validated pre-filtering on an index, set the default index mode on the vector bucket so that new indexes use ENHANCED without a follow-up call:

To bring the rest of your existing indexes across, list them and check the index mode on each one, then call UpdateIndexMode on the ones still using CLASSIC:

Now available Metadata pre-filtering is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. You pay standard S3 Vectors pricing for storage, PUT requests, and queries. For full pricing details, visit the Amazon S3 pricing page. For regional availability, visit Amazon S3 Vectors Regions and quotas.

Whether you’re scoping a RAG application to one tenant, scoping an agent’s searches to one user’s documents, or narrowing a catalog search to a licensing window, pre-filtering lets you apply those filters without trading away recall. To learn more and get started, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation. Send feedback to AWS re:Post for S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#10007. Nvidia is happy to take your money whether you're using open or closed models, says Jensen Huang

At Fireworks Forge, a celebration of specialized models

Nvidia doesn't seem to care whether open or closed models win out as long as its hardware is powering the infrastructure.

"We love closed models," CEO Jensen Huang said. "There's a solid place in the world for closed frontier models. But the world has so many good ideas … The idea that all of us would be based on general intelligence is not logical."

Speaking with Lin Qiao, CEO and founder of Fireworks.ai, at the company's Forge event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Huang wasn't ready to throw Nvidia's cloud customers, which help deliver the proprietary AI of Anthropic and OpenAI, under the onrushing open model bus.

But having come to the defense of open weight models in July to push back against protectionist pressure from the leadership of Anthropic and OpenAI, Huang recognizes the economic and strategic appeal of AI services that are more affordable and less locked-in.

Most of the value in the world, he said, is captured in specialized intelligence, which is to say AI models trained on specific domains of knowledge.

"The opportunity for artificial superintelligence is already here," he said. "By taking an open frontier model, adapting it, and providing it with your domain knowledge, your access to your specialized tools, and the proper evaluation, you should be able to create essentially a superintelligence."

That aligns with Fireworks' business – offering a platform for companies to train and run models tuned to their specific needs. Coincidentally, that platform just received an infusion of 25,000 Nvidia GPUs to support its expansion in Europe.

Huang's endorsement of open models also fits with Qiao's introductory remarks about the need for the AI frontier to be open. But he largely avoided echoing Qiao's focus on the cost savings allowed by working with open models.

In her introductory remarks, Qiao stood on stage backlit by a slide composed of ten headlines highlighting the extraordinary cost of unchecked token spending.

"Cost is out of control," she said. "Business cannot scale without borrowing a lot of money."

That theme was echoed in a subsequent session helmed by Kay Zhu, co-founder and CTO of AI workspace Genspark, titled Gen-1 Slides: Frontier Quality Without Frontier Costs. Gen-1 Slides, Genspark's model for generating slide decks, was built atop MiniMax M3 and tuned to deliver results comparable to Anthropic's Opus 5 at 1/17th the cost – $0.30/M tokens compared to $5/M.

Asked what might become commonplace next year but seems unlikely today, Huang said this year's breakthrough has been agent harnesses that turn AI models into agents. He added, "I would say the big breakthrough we'll talk about next year, maybe this is a little self-serving, is how Open Shell has enabled every company in the world to deploy agents safely, confidently."

Given the nod to make a second prediction, Huang added, "I would say that the second big breakthrough for industry would be hardware in the loop. And hardware in the loop basically is robotic systems."

Given Nvidia's evident interest and investment in robotics, that would be fortuitous. ®

#10005. Amazon S3 Tables now support all Apache Iceberg V3 data types

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Amazon S3 Tables now support all data types in the Apache Iceberg V3 specification. You can create V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables to take advantage of V3 features like deletion vectors, row lineage, and new data types such as variant, nanosecond timestamps, unknown, geometry, and geography.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for managing large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data in open Parquet files in data lakes on object storage like Amazon S3. Amazon S3 Tables offer storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with fully managed features like automatic compaction, maintenance, replication, and Intelligent-Tiering.

Teams running analytics on Apache Iceberg V2 tables often hit the same limits as their data grows. A compliance request to delete 50,000 user records from a 2-billion-row table leaves behind positional delete files that slow queries until compaction runs. Semi-structured events land as JSON strings that every query has to parse. Geospatial coordinates and nanosecond-precision timestamps get encoded as strings or integers. Each workaround adds storage cost, query latency, and pipeline code. With V3, Iceberg solves these challenges by offering native support for semi-structured and geospatial data, faster row-level operations, and built-in row lineage for data governance.

Starting today, Amazon S3 Tables support all V3 data types, including variant, nanosecond timestamps, geometry, geography, and unknown, along with deletion vectors and row lineage. You can create new V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables in place, and S3 Tables continue to run compaction and maintenance for you.

Apache Iceberg V3 V3 is the latest version of the Iceberg specification. Among its many improvements, V3 introduces capabilities that address the most common pain points in V2. This includes:

Deletion vectors replace V2’s positional delete files with a compact binary format. That 50,000-row compliance delete now writes a single deletion vector file instead of thousands of small deletes, significantly reducing compaction time and delete file overhead.

Row lineage adds _row_id and _last_updated_sequence_number to each record automatically. Your downstream pipelines can query these fields to find changed rows without scanning the full table.

New data types let you store semi-structured, geospatial, and nanosecond-precision data natively instead of encoding it as strings or integers:

Variant data type stores semi-structured data in columnar format. During writes, the engine shreds variant data into hidden columns and collects statistics. At query time, those statistics enable file pruning that significantly reduces I/O compared to parsing JSON strings.

The following sections walk through how to use these V3 capabilities in practice, with examples that show how to create tables, work with the new data types, and manage data at scale.

Getting started A retail analytics team tracks user behavior across web and mobile apps. Each event has a different structure: page views include URLs and duration, purchases include items and amounts, and searches include query terms and result counts. With V3’s variant type, you store all event shapes in one table without predefined schemas:

Insert events with different payload shapes without worrying about schema evolution:

Now query the variant column directly, without PARSE_JSON at read time. With Amazon EMR Spark, use variant_get:

To enable deletion vectors for write operations, configure merge-on-read mode:

Now when you run a compliance delete, V3 writes a small deletion vector instead of rewriting data files:

S3 Tables compaction handles these deletion vector files automatically on the next maintenance cycle.

Upgrading from V2 AWS provides backwards compatibility for both versions to minimize disruption during migration to V3. Existing V2 readers continue to work on upgraded tables until you’re ready to fully adopt V3 features. For more details, see the S3 Tables Iceberg V3 documentation. Upgrade an existing table atomically without rewriting data:

On the next compaction cycle, S3 Tables remove old V2 delete files. New modifications use deletion vectors automatically. Row lineage fields initialize on the first data modification after the upgrade.

This is a one-way operation. The Apache Iceberg specification does not support downgrading from V3 to V2. Verify that all engines accessing the table support V3 before upgrading.

Using row lineage for incremental pipelines After your table has V3 data, use row lineage to build efficient incremental pipelines:

This returns only rows modified after sequence number 42. Your downstream jobs can checkpoint this value and process only new changes on each run, instead of scanning the full table.

Compatibility across AWS analytics services AWS offers the broadest native Apache Iceberg support of any major cloud provider, with Iceberg-compatible services at every layer of the data stack: ingestion, storage, catalog, and analytics. You can store and automatically optimize V3 tables in Amazon S3 Tables, write data with Amazon EMR Spark, integrate and manage data with AWS Glue, and run analytics with Amazon Redshift. To learn more about AWS analytics support for V3, see the Apache Iceberg on AWS prescriptive guidance.

Both S3 Tables and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) API, enabling interoperability across engines regardless of the catalog endpoint.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables support for all Apache Iceberg V3 data types is now available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables are supported. Apache Iceberg V3 support is available at no additional charge; standard S3 Tables pricing applies.

To get started, visit the Amazon S3 Tables documentation or create a table bucket from the Amazon S3 console. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Send feedback to AWS re:Post or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#10003. Announcing AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered intelligence to optimize your cloud environment (preview)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing the public preview of AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered service that analyzes your AWS environment to deliver targeted, contextual recommendations for improving your applications’ cost, security, performance, and resilience. The AWS Well-Architected Agent analyzes your infrastructure, understands unique business goals, and delivers contextual recommendations with ready-to-implement fixes. It delivers context-aware optimization without relying on manual audits or generic checklists.

The agent evaluates your environment as an experienced cloud architect would. It automatically correlates utilization metrics, resource configurations, and application topology, and analyzes against Well-Architected best practices across 65+ AWS services. It generates recommendations aligned to your declared business goals, delivers implementation packages with every finding, and surfaces cross-pillar trade-offs making it simpler to remediate the findings.

Here are the three main features of this service:

AWS Well-Architected Agent in action To get started, create an agent profile to define the scope of what Well-Architected Agent can access and provide recommendations on, complete the IAM role setup to access resources, conduct architecture review, and remediate recommendations.

Create an agent profile In the AWS Well-Architected console, choose Get started with Well-Architected Agent. You can define an agent profile that specifies which AWS accounts and applications to monitor, which optimization pillars to focus on, and the permissions required.

You can choose AWS accounts or AWS Regions to monitor and optimization pillars that matter most to your business. You can also set goals for each pillar: cost optimization, performance, resilience, and security.

To give access to the agent for your AWS environment, provision customer-managed IAM roles the agent uses to read resource configurations, utilization metrics, and application topology. To learn more, visit the IAM prerequisite for AWS Well-Architected Agent.

When you choose Get Started, the agent creates your agent profile. Resource and application recommendations will be generated within 24 hours after profile creation.

You can conduct an architecture review on pre-deployment workloads by uploading an IaC project in Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) to be analyzed. Choose Conduct architecture review in the dashboard, upload a.zip file containing IaC project or repository file, and select which Well-Architected lens to use for reviewing your infrastructure.

You can define your applications to add context which will enhance the relevancy and further contextualize recommendations. Choose Add application context in the dashboard, add your applications with AWS accounts, AWS Regions, AWS services, tags if you want to narrow the scope to specific resources, and the details of applications.

Review prioritized recommendations and start remediating Now you can see generated prioritized recommendations generated by the agent across your resources and applications, selected pillars, ranked against your declared goals, with automation-ready remediation included.

When you choose the specific recommendation, you can see the details, insights into why the agent are suggesting the recommendation, impacts and trade-off, and recommended fixes across affected AWS resources.

Choose Start remediation to address recommended fixes. You can choose the console, updated IaC template, CLI commands to remediate by the resolution type. It provides detailed step-by-step instructions and you can roll out this instruction and verify the result.

When you choose Using updated IaC template, the agent provides the code changes needed to update your existing IaC templates such as the CDK function shown above which you can copy directly into your codebase.

You can also configure API access to integrate recommendations directly into your existing development and operations workflows. To interact with the agent programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the AWS Well-Architected Agent documentation.

Things to know Here are some things that you should know about the Well-Architected Agent.

You can still use existing AWS Well-Architected Tool to manually evaluate your cloud architecture with user-defined lenses that measure your workload using your own best practices.

Join the preview Access to the AWS Well-Architected Agent and its recommendations is available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). You can onboard workloads from any AWS commercial Region. AWS Well-Architected Agent is delivered by AWS Support and available to AWS customers with an AWS Support plan.

Give it a try today in the AWS Well-Architected console and send feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#9998. Microsoft improves Windows 11 performance on 8 GB PCs as RAM prices keep climbing

We've got a hunch the memory crunch is taking a bite out of Windows revenue

With RAM getting more expensive, Microsoft is putting more effort into making Windows 11 run better on systems with just 8 GB of memory.

Microsoft said on Tuesday that it was "raising the bar for 8 GB Windows 11 PCs," following a renewed focus on memory optimization earlier this year. The changes come as Redmond continues pushing more expensive Copilot+ PCs, which require at least 16 GB of RAM, amid a memory crunch fueled by AI infrastructure demand.

Now, Microsoft says a low-end machine with its 8 GB of precious RAM will be up to 20 percent more responsive and 40 percent faster at multitasking thanks to improvements made in memory management.

The tweaks are relatively simple, as Microsoft explained, and seem more about adjusting back to the reality that its flagship operating system needs to function on the hardware people can actually afford to purchase if and when they’re forced to upgrade.

Windows 11 will now keep up to 2 GB more active data in memory before shunting it to slower storage, as one example. In another instance, Windows will connect directly to Edge when the browser is already running in the background, allowing it to launch up to 33 percent faster, according to Microsoft. Microsoft apps are also being made more efficient, with Teams able to enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which Microsoft said will make it launch "up to 20 percent faster."

Memory efficiency is also being improved by tweaking things like Widgets, which will only load when used instead of always being on, and decreasing the time when Edge tabs go to sleep from two hours to 15 minutes by default. Microsoft said it’s enabling third-party apps to make use of those tweaks, too.

Microsoft also included benchmark data in the blog post from a recent bit of research it commissioned. The benchmark report compares a range of 2026 Windows machines with models from 2021, finding that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8 GB of RAM performed about as well as a 2021 Dell XPS 13 with 16 GB across selected workloads.

What that means, says Microsoft, is that “the complete PC, not memory capacity alone, shapes the experience.”

In other words, please buy some new Windows hardware, even if it’s expensive - we’re begging you. Software optimization can only do so much.

“For many people, 8 GB is a great fit for the things they do every day,” Microsoft EVP of Windows and devices Pavan Davuluri wrote in the blog post. “Demanding workloads, such as 3D modeling, advanced video editing, or large-scale data processing benefit from 16 GB of memory or more.”

It’s no surprise Microsoft is improving the performance of lower end systems at the same time it’s subtly asking users to buy newer kit, even if it’s just an 8 GB machine - Microsoft may have done well in the past two quarters, but it’s no thanks to Windows devices.

Microsoft’s Q4 2026 earnings in late July saw the company rake in cash more broadly, while simultaneously reporting a 7 percent decrease in Windows OEM and devices revenue.

Likewise, in its fiscal Q1 2027 results, reported just last week, Microsoft again brought home a mountain of net income, with adjusted earnings reaching $36.4 billion, up 18 percent from the same period last year. Windows OEM and devices revenue, however, was down a whopping 22 percent. It’s hard to think of a reason beyond the fact that hardware prices have shot up with more force than a SpaceX rocket - memory prices are likely to actually make it to Mars, unlike Starship - leaving both consumers and enterprises to stretch those upgrade cycles.

If you need to get the most out of that 8 GB Windows 11 PC, you’ll find the latest improvements in 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later. Microsoft is also encouraging users to keep its branded apps up to date, as “some improvements arrive through app updates or through Microsoft Store.”  ®
