#9969. AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions, which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it.

The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesOpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex.

AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate, which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate, which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher.

AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs.

Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2, and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR, point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks: lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x.

Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service, producing the evidence its regulator needed.

How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog.

Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

#9967. Datacenter operators must win hearts and minds, not just permits

Schneider sees no slowdown despite backlash, but says communities deserve answers on power, water, and noise

Schneider Electric sees no slowdown in its datacenter business, but says operators must be more open with communities about the power, water, and land their projects will consume.

As a supplier of electrical infrastructure, cooling, and power distribution equipment, Schneider has a direct view of operators' spending plans – and a commercial interest in continued construction.

Steven Carlini, vice president of innovation and datacenter, said Schneider's pipeline showed no slowdown. "And Schneider has a lot of agreements, supply chain agreements with the larger datacenter operators."

Reports earlier this year suggested only half the capacity planned for 2026 is actually under construction in the US, and land being cleared for new bit barn projects has plateaued.

Carlini nevertheless said US companies were building as fast as they could, contrasting that with planning bureaucracy and other obstacles in Europe.

"But the one thing that I think is going to be the biggest change is the level of transparency from the operators when they're trying to secure permits and when they're requesting power," Carlini said.

"The way the model traditionally worked in the US is the operators would negotiate with the local jurisdictions that were responsible for issuing the permits, and there would be non-disclosures involved, almost universally. So the residents where these datacenters were going to be built had no visibility into these projects until construction started."

Opposition to datacenter construction has grown in the US. Campaign groups called for a moratorium on new facilities late last year, and New York state imposed a halt this summer.

The sheer scale of the new builds has also alarmed many folk, with Meta's Hyperion facility, for example, planned to reach 5 GW of power capacity and cover an area equal to a significant chunk of Manhattan.

A recent survey by think tank Pew Research Center found that Americans are increasingly wary of datacenters, with more than half saying they are bad for the environment, bad for household energy bills, and consume water resources for cooling.

In response, companies building and operating compute sheds need to be more upfront about what effect their plans will have on the local area, Carlini said.

"They're going to have to disclose where the power is going to come from, how they're going to get the power, their water usage, their carbon emissions, the efficiency of the datacenter, where it is going to be located physically, the noise levels of the facility, the water sources, which is a big one, and how much water they're going to use is another big one that operators have traditionally not been very forthright in publishing."

In Virginia – the world's "datacenter capital" – an ex-water sustainability program manager at AWS is taking his former employer to court over claims it published false and misleading statements about water use in the state.

Carlini expects permitting requirements to force greater disclosure, followed by reporting obligations once facilities are operating.

"And then they're going to have to report it as part of regulations during operations as well, so it's not going to be a case of here's our prediction, and then you get the permit and you never have to report again," he said.

Datacenter owners and operators must win hearts and minds as well, Carlini added, a point already recognized by some in the industry at an event last year.

"From a public relations perspective, that's another area where the operators really need to focus, because in many cases they've taken the position that they're benefiting the community," he said. "Those days are gone, so the operators are going to have to, from a PR perspective, engage with the local residents more amicably."

People using Facebook or Gmail doesn't mean they'll welcome a datacenter next door, Carlini told us.

"So it's going to have to be more like 'Here's how we're going to help,'" he said. Operators would need to acknowledge residents' concerns and explain any benefits, such as tax breaks or lower costs.

For AI facilities, Carlini expects more attention to token-processing performance and efficiency, rather than power capacity alone.

"I think we're going to start to see more and more focus on tokens per watt, tokens per dollar, and even datacenters could be sized in tokens as a performance metric for the IT rather than just the power metric," he told us.

"I think the industry has suffered in the past because datacenters have always just been sized in power consumption, and that gave little idea what it was producing and what value [it] was adding."

For more on the economics of tokens in AI processing, readers can refer to our article on this topic from earlier this year. ®

#9966. Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in.

What is new Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation.

S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline.

Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier.

A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console, then choose Create table from migration.

Create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency.

When you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write.

You can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation.

You can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or the Agent Toolkit for AWS. For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command.

To catch up the destination table with changes in the source, call sync-table-migration as many times as you need before you complete the migration. Each sync copies only what changed.

If you’re using coding agents like Kiro, the migrating-hive-tables-to-s3-tables skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS provides step-by-step migration guidance with safety guardrails for agents. The skill can:

To learn more, visit the GitHub README page for the skill.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables managed migration is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm) Regions. At launch, the capability supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, or troubleshoot about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

Try it in the Amazon S3 console today and send feedback to AWS re:Post for Amazon S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.

#9963. Windows pushed AI PCs, but now it's hit a wall of RAM prices

Customers sweating assets amid tight budgets, as Microsoft execs get creative with sales pitches

Microsoft wants enterprise customers to start thinking about PC refreshes using the same mindset – and line in the budget – as AI investments. The problem? Rising component costs caused by the proliferation of AI datacenters mean many clients are delaying client refreshes.

In a call to arms, Microsoft became the headline sponsor of the Canalys Forum in Barcelona early last month for the first time ever. Redmond needs distributors and resellers that convene at the event annually to get behind Copilot, Cowork and, more generally, AI computers.

Mark Linton, corporate veep for Windows and Device Sales, took to the stage to preach to a room he is hoping to convert.

"What we're seeing is the tokenomics of [AI] is getting very challenging," he said. "Having agents working on frontier models quickly becomes very expensive."

Redmond's proposed solution is to use those massive LLMs where most needed, "the right model for the right job," running smaller models locally at the edge on Windows PCs. "My goal, if we're successful in pivoting Windows to the agentic platform, is to have PC spend be part of the AI spend versus just PC refresh budget," he said.

"In an AI hybrid world, you'll be able to use edge devices, powerful PCs with lots of memory, lots of capability to run your AI workloads that are appropriate right there on the device. You keep the data locally. Of course, you don't have the token cost of the cloud. You have better latency, and you have more control."

Copilot is merely a component. This is not only about customers using Microsoft "first-party software" – it's for all models and all agents to use Windows as the platform, added Linton.

Goodness knows, Windows does need a shot in the arm. Microsoft last week reported profit and loss accounts for Q1 of its fiscal 2027, ended September 30, and revenue in the Windows OEM and Devices division shrank 22 percent from last year to $3.55 billion. Microsoft warned revenue generated in its Q2 may be down 30 percent.

"Growth will continue to be impacted by elevated inventory levels, PC market demand and a prior year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support," Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on an earnings call.

Market watcher IDC said calendar Q3 PC shipments sank to 62.7 million units, down 20.1 percent year-on-year, translating into 15.8 million fewer sales into distributors' warehouses. Tough macroeconomic conditions coupled with rising memory costs mean tough times for the PC industry.

Omdia – which owns Canalys – said: "The impact of upstream component cost increases has now fully worked its way through to end-market pricing, with consumers and IT decision-makers responding accordingly."

Reg readers know why component costs are going up. The datacenter construction frenzy meant memory chip makers could make more money from higher-margin HBM than conventional DRAM, prompting them to prioritize production of the former.

But AI PCs have been a tough sell from the start, as higher prices and a lack of killer applications meant many customers delayed purchases. Microsoft has to convince the market of the benefits – including trade customers as well as those in charge of procurement at enterprises.

Back at the Canalys Forum, Microsoft's Linton claimed customers mulling AI PC purchases want better productivity, to reduce costs, to innovate, and to be able to use these computers securely and at scale.

Microsoft is going to invest heavily in Windows from both the platform capability and security to enable these ends. So, if you are a Microsoft partner, you'll be able to run Windows and secure agents at the operating system level with Agent 365, with Intune, or with Entra.

Linton added: "We announced in June some of the technology in Windows, in particular Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC). And so essentially you can virtualize agents, and then you can use Intune to give them policy. And so other platforms, you have to manage agent by agent. Windows, you'll be able to do it policy-based, much like you manage people and network resources.

"You will have agents for all, and you need to know how to manage them, track them, audit them, and then ensure that they're contained in the right way. So we're doing that at the operating system primitive level."

Some of the quality control issues that have dogged Windows may give some sysadmins pause for thought about the grand claims made by the Windows exec.

Still, Microsoft is on a mission, and it knows how to attract thousands of resellers by dangling financial incentives in their direction. Linton said it is pumping money into channel programs, including AI-readiness funded headcount with "top partners" to "get this hybrid AI story moving."

Microsoft wants the channel to deploy AI internally too, "especially for your sales team" because "if they're using it, they're able to sell it."

Dell isn’t hopeful of an uplift in PC demand this year. David Kennedy, chief financial officer, said sales will remain "compressed."

"The reality is most enterprises this year for their IT budgets are sweating those assets out a little bit more and what dollars they have, they're trying to build out their infrastructure side," he told the Citi TMT conference in September.

"As we go forward, I think you'll see it [become] a little bit more robust. Our main focus will be on those higher ASP (average sales price) commercial boxes as part of the AI storyboard that's there."

He reckons there are more than 400 million PCs owned by customers that are "over four years old", and with the "cheapest token being closest to the data, none of those installed base PCs will have the battery life or the power to do AI workloads on them. So there is a pent-up demand that we believe will come once it stabilizes and once IT budgets get a little bit more settled and expanded."

Will 2027 be the year of the AI desktop? The Reg suspects not, though readers can do what they always do and speak their brains in the comments section.  ®

Put native GitHub features to work to review outside collaborator access and archive stale repositories.

Working with outside collaborators can add more work for a repository owner. You need to confirm who still needs access, change permissions as projects evolve, and archive repositories once they’ve served their purpose.

To keep up, repository owners need to track collaborators, deadlines, and follow-ups for each repository. As a project grows, that manual housekeeping becomes harder to keep up with and easier to defer.

We faced this problem in a shared organization where GitHub employees (“Hubbers”) collaborate with customers and partners on product trials and professional services engagements. Our answer was Evergreen, a GitHub App built with native GitHub features. The workflows below exhibit a pattern you can adapt for your own organization.

Evergreen is a GitHub App that automates organization hygiene through two workflows:

Fail secure. If nobody responds to an access review, we don’t leave access in place and hope for the best. We revoke it. The safe outcome is the default outcome.

Never destroy anything. Evergreen will never delete a repository or its contents. Archived repos are recoverable, and every access change is written into the repo’s tracking issue, so reverting a mistake is as easy as a copy-paste to Copilot.

Under the hood, Evergreen is a small Go webhook server running in a container. But the interesting part is the choreography. Every moving piece is a stock GitHub feature: a GitHub App, scheduled actions, webhooks, issues, custom properties, and plain files in a repo. Nothing exotic to reinvent.

A dedicated controller repo acts as Evergreen’s clock and its memory. Four scheduled GitHub Actions workflows fire repository_dispatch events on a quarterly cadence, and the app wakes up and does the work:

Reviews open two weeks before their cleanup runs, and there’s a hard grace period baked in so a stray manual run can never fast‑forward the guillotine. Each workflow also supports workflow_dispatch, so we can trigger any step by hand as needed.

Evergreen tracks every repo’s status as a JSON file (one per repository) committed to the controller repo under state/repos/.json. The snapshot of who had access, when the review opened, the deadline, who decided, and what happened all lives there. Here’s a completed review where a Hubber kept Alice’s access and let Bob’s lapse:

The best part: because state is just files in git, the commit history is the audit trail. Want to know why someone lost access last spring? git log the state file. There’s no separate database or bespoke audit pipeline to track.

Evergreen does its talking through issues inside each repository. When an access review kicks off, every repo gets a checklist issue:

The interaction model is delightfully simple: check the boxes for who stays, then close the issue. That’s it. When the issue closes, Evergreen listens for the issues.closed webhook event, reads the checkboxes, retains the checked collaborators, and revokes the rest, then posts a receipt comment listing exactly what it kept and what it removed.

Closing an access review issue is a privileged action, so Evergreen guards it. If someone who isn’t a Hubber closes an issue, the app quietly reopens it and posts a note explaining why. Decisions only count when they come from the people authorized to make them.

Here’s a subtle problem: we know the people who need to respond to a review are Hubbers, but we didn’t always know which Hubber(s) owned a given repository.

Evergreen resolves the right people to notify through a fallback chain:

The result: the right owners get pinged automatically, without anyone maintaining a spreadsheet of “who owns what.”

When a review deadline passes with no response, cleanup revokes every collaborator in the snapshot. We were careful about a subtle edge case: what if some removals succeed while others hit a transient API error? Marking the review “done” while a removal is still outstanding would be a quiet inconsistency, and we didn’t want that.

So Evergreen fails closed. If any removal fails, the review stays pending and the issue stays open, and the next run retries the stragglers. It only records “revoked” once every removal actually succeeded. And whatever gets removed is written into the issue, so restoring access is a matter of re‑adding the handles it listed.

Automated housekeeping has a reputation for being the office smoke alarm: loud, easy to ignore, and usually going off while you’re cooking something perfectly fine. We worked hard to make Evergreen feel like the opposite:

Automation that manages access and archives repositories deserves a careful rollout, especially into a large, active org (ours has 1,400+ Hubbers, and many more customers and partners). We wanted the very first run to be a complete non‑event. A few practices got us there:

Dry‑run first. Evergreen ships with a DRY_RUN mode that logs every write it would make without touching a single collaborator or repo. We ran it against the real org and read the logs like tea leaves until we trusted the decisions it wanted to make.

Overcommunicate. Before flipping the switch, we broadcast what was coming, when, and what people needed to do, so the first issue anyone saw wasn’t a surprise. We found that when you’re telling a large group the same thing for the seventh time, it’s often when many are still hearing it for the first time.

Watch everything with Splunk. Evergreen emits structured logfmt logs to a dedicated Splunk index. That observability is how we caught edge cases in the wild (empty collaborator lists, unusual permissions, repos with issues disabled) and tightened the logic before they mattered.

Respect the platform’s speed limits. When you open issues and post comments across every repo in a big org, you slam into GitHub’s secondary rate limits for content creation: 80 requests/minute and 500/hour. While this is a thoughtful preventative control to avoid system abuse, it requires a bit of intention when automating IssueOps at large scale.

So Evergreen paces itself by construction. It processes repos in batches, spaces out each content‑creating call by a couple of seconds, and sleeps between batches to let the rolling window clear, and it only counts the repos that actually create content, so a quiet quarter where nothing’s eligible still runs fast. We opted for proactive avoidance over reactive back‑off.

Routine hygiene is the kind of work that’s easy to defer and perfect to automate. The trick isn’t heroic cleanup sprints: it’s making the boring, safe thing happen on a schedule, with a friendly face and an undo button.

That’s Evergreen. And because it’s built entirely from native GitHub features, you can stand up the same pattern yourself.

Ready to make repository hygiene routine? Start with one recurring access or archival task, then use GitHub Apps, actions, issues, and custom properties to automate the problem away.

Senior Service Delivery Engineer at GitHub, passionate about the intersection of software engineering & security, and helping businesses focus on innovation, growth, and speed to market.

#9959. Achieving nirvana: Enlightenment 0.28 hits the desktop

Very nearly 30something environment gets spruced up… and there's a new Trinity, too

Fresh on the desktop this week is a new version of Enlightenment as well the continuation of noughties hero KDE 3, the Trinity Desktop Environment, for those who prefer things a little old school.

Enlightenment version 0.28 is the latest release of one of the older Linux graphical environments, which first appeared in 1997. Version 0.28 arrives nearly two years after the previous release – we reported on Enlightement 0.27 in January 2025. If you're not familiar with this venerable window manager, often referred to as just E, we refer you back to that article, which also explains Enlightenment's slightly strange version numbering scheme.

Last time around we noted that its single-line release notes really didn't give us much to write about. The development team has made up for it this time, with some 68 lines of changes. It's both the same old E, and simultaneously a modern tool: it is still an X11 window manager, but it can also act as a Wayland compositor if you prefer. It offers conventional stacking resizable windows, but also can act as a tiling window manager if you prefer. On recent distros, it can now talk to the Pipewire audio server, and it can also work with NetworkManager to control network connections. This version delivers preliminary support for NetBSD too.

This isn't really a tool for newbies or those looking for a simple easy desktop. A sign of its age is that the first-run wizard asks if you want windows to activate as soon as you move the mouse pointer over them. This was traditional 20th century Unix behavior, and in the early days of Linux it was called "focus-follows-mouse," but it's rarely seen today. E isn't a full desktop environment: it only offers a few of its own optional tools, such as the Ecrire text editor, Ephoto picture viewer, Evisum task manager, and Rage video player. Even its taskbar is optional. It is more like a basis for experienced users to customize and build their own environment around.

The Trinity Desktop Environment has a rather lower learning curve: TDE is a port of the final version of KDE 3 to modern Linux. Proving old school is still cool, the project – which keeps the look and feel of 2005-era KDE 3.5 alive – has just announced TDE release 14.1.7, with dozens of bug fixes and plenty of new features. Among these is a tweak to the kicker/taskbar: you can now scroll the taskbar using the mouse wheel, flicking through your open applications.This release drops support for Ubuntu 24.10 "Oracular Oriole" but adds support for the latest 26.10 "Stonking Stingray."

Forks of older versions by users disenchanted with new versions are a recurring feature of the FOSS world, but they often tend to peter out after a while. TDE is one of the exceptions: we first reported on a new release in 2021 and again in 2023. ®

#9957. 'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

An ongoing supply chain attack is harvesting credentials and sensitive data from thousands of developer repositories.

An ongoing attack is abusing compromised GitHub tokens to harvest cloud secrets and credentials from thousands of developer repositories, bringing into focus how compromised developer accounts can provide a gateway into enterprise cloud environments.

Dubbed "Gheist," the campaign has left more than 13,500 malicious branches — or versions of a project's code — across more than 850 compromised GitHub accounts, according to a report published over the weekend by Wiz Research.

The campaign affects everything from personal projects to private enterprise repositories, although public repositories are protected by safeguards GitHub introduced in July, according to the report.

"The control GitHub added is focused on protecting public repositories from workflow abuse vectors," Wiz researcher Rami McCarthy tells Dark Reading. However, "once an enterprise credential is compromised, that control doesn’t apply," he adds.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Wiz also found overlap between Gheist-affected GitHub accounts and other abuse campaigns, including repository-based malware distribution, attempts to exploit GitHub Actions for computing resources, and possible infections linked to other malware operations.

This overlap — which distinguishes Gheist from similar campaigns — suggests stolen developer tokens may be reused or shared among threat actors, "demonstrating the complexity and activity of this threat landscape," McCarthy says.

The campaign relies on a workflow named "sync-check," which is committed to each repository accessible through a stolen token, the researchers wrote.

"The workflow seeks to print the repository’s secrets into its own workflow log," they wrote. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent 'gheist,' which gives the campaign its name."

Wiz began tracking the activity Sept. 15 and said the operation remains active and evolving as of Oct. 24. The researchers reported the activity to GitHub, and about two-thirds of the implicated accounts are no longer available, which "likely indicates response activity," according to the report.

The tokens appear to have come primarily from two sources: infostealer malware and credentials exposed in earlier software supply chain compromises, the researchers noted.

GitHub tokens authorize users and applications to access repositories, code, and administrative functions, making them valuable to attackers seeking to compromise projects and organizations.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens to create branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters. The attackers then add the GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, using the commit message "ci: sync config," according to the report.

"The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner," the researchers wrote. The resulting push event triggers a workflow that attempts to print environment variables and repository secrets into its log. The attack encodes the output using Base32 before retrieving the logs through the GitHub API and deleting the workflow run seconds later.

"Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block," the researchers explained.

A key finding is that Wiz observed successful attacks in private repositories and enterprise environments, where the public-repository safeguard did not apply. Most GitHub-targeted activity, by contrast, primarily affects public repositories, McCarthy tells Dark Reading.

"The attack succeeded in the environments organizations considered safest because a credential issued to a human months ago still carried full write authority," says James Matchett, head of security at supply chain security firm Cloudsmith, in an email interview. "'Private' is not a control. Scoped, short-lived credentials, a tight inventory of what can push and pull, and the discipline to rotate after every incident are the control.”

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

Wiz observed the attackers cycling through tokens belonging to multiple users and automation accounts, and cloning private repositories before planting malicious workflows. Within hours, cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager, the researchers added.

Wiz estimates that the campaign affected "on the scale of a dozen companies," McCarthy says. However, "we have not seen consistent or automated abuse outside of mass cloning of GitHub repositories and the core credential theft," he says.

Token abuse is an increasingly common way for attackers to infiltrate organizations through the developer pipeline. Research presented at Black Hat Europe last year found that some of the most significant software supply chain incidents over the preceding year involved threat actors exploiting GitHub flaws. Defenders therefore must treat developer projects as critical organizational assets.

To defend against Gheist and other forms of token abuse, Wiz urged security teams to hunt for malicious GitHub Actions workflows, rotate exposed secrets, and treat compromised self-hosted runners as potential infrastructure breaches.

More specifically, defenders should look for branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters, where the only change is a new .github/workflows/sync-check.yml file with the commit message "ci: sync config," the researchers advised. Administrators also should review GitHub audit logs for workflow runs on "ci-sync-*" branches that were deleted within a minute of completion, as well as activity from the user agent "gheist."

For broader protection against GitHub token abuse, Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at security firm Secure.com, recommends that organizations "replace long-lived personal access tokens with GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens" and "require reviewers on any environment that holds production secrets." These measures can help limit attackers' ability to access sensitive credentials even if they obtain valid tokens.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9955. Cyberattack on French plasma stores is enough to make your blood boil

Attackers reportedly set cold-room controls to 110°C, but safeguards prevented stock losses

Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said.

The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products.

The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion.

"The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said.

"Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities."

The EFS did not name the supplier publicly.

According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature.

The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health.

News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes.

Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food.

The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday.

Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed.

Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain.

No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting.

The latest wave of cold-store attacks comes a month after the first, which affected French supermarket chains Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others.

Both supermarket waves involved remote interference with refrigeration controls, causing stock losses. Whether the attack affecting EFS used the same access route remains unclear.

Some affected chains identified Danfoss controllers in their systems; others said they did not use the company's equipment.

CERT-FR published an advisory at the time of the attacks urging organizations to remediate vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers.

The attacks in France followed reports of compromises at US military commissaries, which also led to food wastage in August. ®

AI, agents, voice, and physical controls are shifting software development from operating tools to expressing intent—and helping developers stay focused on building.

For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine.

AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls.

We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different.

AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. The development workflow now is about understanding the structure of codebases, the customer, and what a good solution should feel like.

This makes developers’ jobs even more important, and their time more valuable. It makes judgment more valuable. It makes taste more valuable. An agent can generate three implementations before you finish your tea, but someone still has to decide whether the abstraction belongs, the migration is safe, the tests prove anything useful, and the result solves the problem.

That is the most important change in the craft: the developer remains accountable for the outcome, even as more mechanics are delegated.

So what does this mean for the emerging developer workflow? The goal is to embed AI into the workflow, not beside it. It’s more of an ambient intelligence.

That requires portable context. MCP connects agents to tools and services; repository instructions and skills encode conventions; hooks enforce policy and validate output. Simpler interfaces need explicit context underneath.

I see three layers: modality captures intent; the harness plans and acts; the control plane lets developers inspect, redirect, and approve. The best products connect all three without surrendering control.

Together, they let developers move across text, voice, and physical controls without losing context.

I, and many others in the maker community, have been experimenting with ambient control devices, from inexpensive hackable picture frames to ESP32 devices with screens attached. Agentic coding is past just a keyboard and a terminal into alternative interfaces.

Getting this kind of technology into everyone’s hands is something that I’m very passionate about and so over the past 18 months we’ve been working with Logitech on their MX Keypad and how it can help this new way of working.

The Logitech MX Keypad turns familiar developer actions into programmable inputs to accelerate workflows that are ambient and contextual to the work devs are doing. In GitHub Copilot app, a key can submit a parameterized prompt, open or resume a Copilot session, invoke an IDE command, or trigger a multi-step sequence. The hardware earns its place only when that shortcut removes enough friction to keep you in the code, but still gives you control.

Physical controls work when an action repeats often enough that removing a few steps preserves concentration. Not every developer needs another device on the desk, and not every interruption deserves a key. However, with this experience the developer decides which actions earn that shortcut and when the keyboard, command palette, or voice is better. Maintaining flow is the key, and a good interface gives some of that attention back.

GUIs made software visual. Mouse made navigation easier. The web made it connected. Mobile made touch natural. Agents add intent and action. The interface now includes ambient control.

That is why GitHub worked with Logitech to integrate the GitHub Copilot app directly into the experience. Developers can run agentic workflows in control, map a repeated prompt, start or resume a session, and decide through real use whether a physical control helps you stay in flow.

This is still early, so the important questions are engineering questions. How much repository and organizational context should an agent retain? Which tool calls can run automatically? How should credentials, network access, and secrets be scoped? What evidence should accompany a change? How do multiple agents coordinate without duplicating work or creating conflicting pull requests? Products such as MX Keypad let us explore one practical part of that system: how developers invoke, steer, and resume agentic work without losing focus.

For decades, developers learned to speak computer: syntax, commands, APIs, shortcuts, and the occasional incantation copied from a seven-year-old issue comment. Now computers are getting better at meeting us halfway. The best interface will not have the most panels or AI buttons. It will understand enough context, preserve meaningful control, and get out of the way so we can build software that matters.

The goal is not to remove developers from the work. It is to remove friction around the work. Pairing MX Keypad with GitHub Copilot Pro+ gives developers a concrete experiment: choose one repeated interruption, map it to a control, and see whether it preserves focus.

If you want to try it, you can do so here and get three months of GitHub Copilot Pro+.

Learn how to move an agent session from the GitHub Copilot app into VS Code without losing the conversation, code changes, or working context.

The agent has finished the bulk of your change. Now you want to inspect one implementation detail, adjust a few lines by hand, and run the project locally before you ship it.

But the work is sitting in the GitHub Copilot app… and your editor is where you review diffs, debug code, and make final adjustments. Do you have to choose between staying in the session and starting over in Visual Studio Code?

You don’t. You can open the Copilot app session directly in VS Code and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. That means Copilot can handle the repetitive or time-consuming work, then hand control back to you for closer review, hands-on editing, and local testing.

This tutorial assumes you are already comfortable navigating VS Code, running commands in its integrated terminal, and working with Git branches and pull requests.

Open the session you want to continue. Before handing it off, take a moment to review the task and the work Copilot completed.

A session contains more than a collection of modified files. It also records the task, the plan, and the conversation that produced those changes. That context is important when you want to understand why Copilot chose a particular implementation or ask it to revise part of the work.

You do not need to summarize that history or copy it into a new chat before moving to VS Code.

From the session, select Open in VS Code. If the app presents more than one supported editor or VS Code installation, choose the one you want to use.

VS Code opens the project using the worktree associated with the session. It also displays the existing session in the Copilot sidebar.

That gives you three connected pieces of the original work:

You are continuing the existing session, not reconstructing it in a new editor window.

Before editing, inspect the diff in VS Code. Open the Source Control view to see the changed files, then select a file to review its changes line by line.

Review the implementation as you would any other proposed change. In particular, check that:

The preserved conversation can help explain how Copilot arrived at the implementation. If something is unclear, continue prompting Copilot in the sidebar. For example:

You can also ask Copilot to make another change. Because the session and worktree remain connected, you do not have to describe the task from the beginning.

Once you understand the proposed changes, edit any file directly in VS Code.

This is useful for adjustments that are faster or easier to make by hand, such as:

You are editing the session’s existing worktree, so your manual changes build directly on the agent’s work. You do not need to copy files between directories or manually re-create the branch.

Use the VS Code integrated terminal to run the project’s normal validation workflow. The exact commands depend on the repository, but some web app examples may include:

Treat agent-generated changes the same way you would treat code written by a person: run the relevant tests, inspect failures, and verify the behavior yourself.

If the development server prints a localhost URL, open it to test the change in a browser. When supported by your VS Code setup, you can open the URL in VS Code’s integrated browser and inspect the result without leaving the editor.

For a user-interface change, verify both the requested behavior and nearby states. For example, check the modified component at different viewport sizes and confirm that loading, empty, and error states still work.

At any point, you can choose the interaction that best fits the next step:

For example, after making a manual UI adjustment, you might ask Copilot:

Add a test for the updated label and run the relevant test file. Do not modify unrelated components.

Because you are still in the original session, Copilot retains the context needed to interpret “the updated label.”

When the implementation is ready, review the final diff one more time. Then commit and push the changes using the Source Control view or the integrated terminal:

Use your repository’s normal branch, commit, review, and approval practices. Because VS Code opened the worktree and branch associated with the session, pushing the branch updates the pull request already tracking that work.

There is no need to copy the finished files into another checkout or reconnect the work to the pull request manually.

Opening a Copilot app session in VS Code gives you a clean division of labor without splitting the work itself. Copilot can take on a larger or repetitive implementation, while you can move into the editor for detailed review, targeted changes, local testing, and final polish.

The session, diff, and worktree move with you. Start by directing the work in the Copilot app, switch to VS Code whenever you want hands-on control, and push the finished result through the same pull request workflow.

Ready to try it? Download the GitHub Copilot app, start a session, and open it in VS Code when you are ready to continue coding.

#9950. Watchdog sticks probe into Capita's handling of 1.7 million member civil service pension scheme

Public Accounts Committee talks of 'broken promises' and 'chaos' as 'thousands' of retired folk miss out on money

Capita has repeatedly "broken" promises to resolve the "chaos" engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) following its takeover of the administration – a move that left thousands of retired public sector workers unpaid.

So says Parliamentary spending watchdog, the Public Accounts Committee, which this week launched an inquiry into the handover of the ten-year £239 million contract in December from previous incumbent MyCSP.

As The Register exclusively revealed, the troubles began early on as members of CSPS – which manages pensions for 1.7 million people – complained of unrecognized passwords and usernames on the portal Capita developed. Capita said it inherited 132,100 complex remediation cases, and claimed the work-in-progress backlog from the prior system was more than double the 37,000 items when it won the deal in 2023.

Capita ran to Microsoft for support, and promised the use AI and automation, in addition to its 500 full-time employees working on the project, would resolve the issues by March. It missed this deadline, as well as one set for June 30 and is set to miss March 2027.

The government subsequently withheld a £10 million payment to Capita over the CSPS fiasco.

The National Audit Office, a spending regulator, has already launched its own probe into the failures and is now joined by the PAC, which says thousands of civil servants and their families have struggled to on and collect their pensions

The PAC has already held three evidence sessions on Capita and the government’s efforts to ameliorate the situation. The law was changed in the Budget 2026 to mitigate the impact of administrative delays in CSPS on bereaved families.

Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair at the PAC, said in a statement:

"In response to the alarming reports of hard-working civil servants being thrown into financial uncertainty following Capita’s takeover of the CSPS, we have held a number of evidence sessions with both the top leadership of Capita, and the civil servants and ministers of the Cabinet Office who have ultimate responsibility for overseeing the contract.

"Over and over again, promises have been made and broken by Capita, to our faces in formal evidence sessions, that they will get a grip on what has gone wrong. As a result, we are launching an inquiry, which will be informed by the authoritative factual basis provided by the NAO, which supports the scrutiny work of this Committee."

The inquiry will draw on the finding of the NAO's forthcoming report on the switch of CSPS to Capita, and will take into consideration the status of the scheme at go-live date, how Capita has performed, and the effect on CSPS members, plus take a look into the way the Cabinet Office has overseen the prior scheme and the switch to Capita. ®Updated to add at 1407 UTC:Capita has been in touch to say how "deeply sorry" it is about the "frustration" that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme "has caused members and their families." It said it had "made progress," but had a lot more to do. It said its teams are working to resolve outstanding cases "as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

All of this has happened before. All of this will happen again. Maybe

#9949. Is it agentic enough? Benchmarking open models on your own tooling

Benchmarking transformers revisions across different metrics

This is a human-made, agent-focused blogpost.

Coding agents increasingly work with our software instead of us: describe a task, and the agent picks the library, writes the calls, runs them, and debugs its own mistakes. When the library gets in the way, it will happily bypass it and rewrite the logic from scratch. This introduces a new concept in library development: the code should not only be correct and fast, but should be designed so that an agent can drive it effectively. A clunky API or stale docs annoy us developers, but it now also sends the agent down a longer, more expensive path.

Most benchmarks just look at the final answer. We wanted the whole process instead: not just whether the agent got it right, but how much work it took to get there, and how that shifts across models, library revisions, and tasks. We measured exactly that, using transformers as our case study.

Here, we will introduce a tool specific benchmark focusing on how the answer was found, and provide a simple implementation of one such harness, running entirely on open models driven by the pi coding agent, with the full sweep of models × revisions × tasks fanned out across Hugging Face Jobs so every run sees identical hardware.

But, how do you optimize software for agents?

We're strong believers in the following two software principles:

This remains the same within the realm of agentic-optimized tooling, and, for once, the two are directly tied to each other.

You want your tool to exist for an agent: it needs to be discoverable. The API needs to be clear and the docs need to be extensive. They need to be structured in a way that the agent has rapid access to the useful files and examples. If you want your tool to work for an agent, then you should test it for agentic-use.

We'll use transformers as an example throughout this blogpost: agents using it to solve ML tasks (classifying text, captioning images, transcribing audio), not contributing code to it; though the harness was designed to work with any tool that can be operated from the command line.

Our intuition on transformers was that usage could be dramatically simplified with a few changes: a CLI, a Skill, and self-contained, task-specific examples. This is the same recipe recently applied to the hf CLI, redesigned to be agent-optimized, where agents used 1.3–1.8× (and up to 6×) fewer tokens. We wanted to know whether that kind of win generalizes, and whether it could be useful for transformers as well.

Intuition is a powerful tool, but we wanted more evidence before we opened PRs that add several thousand lines of code to such a widely used codebase as transformers. We set out to measure what success looks like.

Two agents can both produce the correct label for a sentiment-classification task, but one:

Both reach POSITIVE (0.9999), and here are the two paths an agent actually took on this exact task:

Both methods reach the same result. But they have very different profiles in cost, latency, token usage, and failures.

If your evaluation only checks the final string, you're blind to these as well as whether a change you shipped to the library (a CLI improvement, better error messages, a Skill) actually helped agents.

Our goal with this harness is to evaluate how much work an agent has to do to perform a given task, and whether changes to the library improve performance.

A few words on how we'll evaluate agents here.

We run every task under three variants (or "tiers"); three different ways an agent can come at transformers:

These aren't nested: skill doesn't contain clone (it ships curated docs, not the source tree), and neither strictly contains the other, each gives the agent a different kind of help. As we'll see, a model can sometimes do better on clone than on skill.

Not all models driving agents are equal, and their difference changes what you should look at when running them.

At one end, you have the largest, most capable open models. On reasonably common tasks, these should get the right answer, eventually. For them, task completion saturates near 100% and stops telling you much about your tool; a more relevant benchmark is the effort it took the agent to get there: how many turns, tokens and seconds it took, and whether they walked a clean path or used deprecated APIs.

Local models vary widely in size, and so do their abilities. Metrics such as "match %" are more relevant than for their larger counterparts, as you can see how model sizes/capabilities affect results on your specific tool.

This harness not only provides guidance to library maintainers on how to improve a repository for agent interactions, it also helps assess how different agents and models perform on the tasks users care about.

The harness scores every run on several axes, so that you can ask what actually matters for each class of model:

All of it lands in a report you can directly examine:

The live report: Overview, Coverage, and Results, all client-side.

And because it captures the native agent trace of every run, numbers are just the beginning: you can read exactly what the agent did, command by command. The traces are shareable through the Hub's agent-traces viewer:

A run rendered in the Hub's agent-traces viewer: MiniMax-M2.7 on the answer-question task. Open this trace on the Hub ↗

Before the results, a quick recap of the setup. Each run varies four things: the model driving the agent, the transformers revision it runs against, the task, and the tier (bare / clone / skill). As discussed, we look at different metrics for the two different model categories.

Since a large open model will usually get to the correct result, what you're really measuring is the effort it took to do so. Did it take ten turns or one? Did it follow an API path you deprecated because it trusted obsolete documentation? Did it hit an error you hadn't foreseen?

The natural experiment is to fix one strong model and vary the tool's revisions: the successive git versions of transformers we test against, from released tags like v5.8.0 and v5.9.0 to the specific commit that introduces the CLI and Skill. We want to watch whether the load it puts on the agent goes up or down. We used the harness on transformers to check whether adding a dedicated CLI and Skill actually lightened the agents' work.

For the three large models we used in our tests, the average time spent on all tasks indicates that the Skill commit results in less time spent working on the tasks:

Median time per revision, by tier: the skill commit (green dot) is the fastest.

On the other hand, in the experiments in which we cloned the repository, we can see a significant increase in token consumption due to the commit that introduced the CLI and examples, as we'll see in a moment.

Median new tokens per revision, by tier: the clone variant jumps once the CLI lands in the repo.

Reading the clone-variant traces explains why. The commit adds a command, but it also ships the CLI's implementation and a set of cli/agentic/*.py usage examples into the repository directly.

On the clone variant the agent has a full transformers checkout in front of it, and roughly a third of the runs go read the new surface (the /cli/ tree and the example scripts) to learn the interface before calling it. This raises the median input from ~4k to ~6.4k tokens.

The two charts are then two sides of one tradeoff: the commit buys the large models less time (they reach for the CLI instead of debugging Python) at the cost of more tokens (they read the code that taught them the CLI). A tradeoff worth knowing about before merging PRs.

One caveat works in the CLI's favor, though, which isn't benchmarked yet: the cost of reading it is amortized with successive runs. Our setup is built for one-off experiments. Each run is a fresh agent that rediscovers the CLI from scratch, so it pays the discovery cost every time. In real usage an agent learns the interface once and then solves task after task within the same session, amortizing that cost across many requests. The token bump we measure here is closer to a worst case than to what a user would see day to day.

Open models give us fine-grained control over the variables that matter most here: size, configuration, quantization, provider, training, and anything that would differ from one model to the next. They're also where a good tool surface matters most: a small model asked to "use transformers to do X" on a bare environment can guess an API that changed some releases ago, may do unnecessary tool calls, and can get the wrong answer.

So here the experiment is the opposite of the above: hold the revision and sweep the model. This helps see which models actually take care of the task, not just by token count and time, but down to which ones can't reliably handle the tool calls. Our intuition is that the smaller the model, the harder both tool use and the task get; we ran the harness across a range of model sizes to test exactly that:

Match % across models, by tier: the skill tier lifts the larger models but drops the smaller ones.

which also seems to be correlated with the number of tokens ingested

Median new tokens across models, by tier.

A note on fair comparison: naively averaging across tasks is misleading when coverage is uneven (a model that only finished the quick tasks looks fast). The report has a "shared tasks only" toggle (across models and/or revisions) so you compare like-for-like, and a Coverage heatmap so you can see exactly which task × revision × model cells actually ran.

Two things come together here: how to look past whether the agent succeeded to what it did and how it did it; as well as the first results we pulled out of the harness.

Match %, tokens, and time tell you the cost of a run but don't tell you much about what happened under the hood.

This is why we've introduced the concept of markers. A marker is a named pattern the profile (the small per-tool plugin that teaches the harness how to build and drive a given library) matches against a run.

It is a one-line label for a behavior you care about, checked against the shell commands the agent ran, the code it wrote, the files it read, or its final answer. A run can fire several markers or none; the report shows how often each one fired, per model and per revision.

For transformers we declare a handful but we'll only look at the two most relevant ones:

These are what we watch to see whether a change actually shifted the agent's behavior. Interestingly here, the larger the model, the more it leverages the new context instead of using its memory; therefore leveraging the newly introduced CLI.

CLI adoption by tier across models: only the skill tier reaches for it, and more so as models grow.

CLI adoption is new: the CLI lands in a single commit, isn't in any model's training data, and is only lightly documented. The effect is clear: it's the Skill variant, the one that ships the CLI's documentation, that actually reaches for it, at 55.3%.

Comparing the commit across model sizes, the CLI + Skill helps the bigger models: on the skill tier, Kimi and the other large agents reach for the CLI and finish in fewer turns. (On clone they spend more input tokens first, reading the new CLI code, as we saw above, so the win shows up in time and turns, not raw tokens.)

Kimi-K2.6, GLM-5.1, and MiniMax-M2.7 across revisions

But in some smaller-model settings, it appears to hurt performance. One plausible explanation is that small models lean on memorized API patterns, reproducing pipeline(...) snippets they've seen in their training data. The new concepts are then a larger surface for them to get wrong. You can watch this directly on the harness: lower match %, more retries, the cli marker barely firing. It is particularly striking on the Qwen3-4B model: the Skill barely changes its match rate yet its cost distribution is significantly affected.

Almost all of that comes from the clone tier. The checkout now contains the CLI's implementation and cli/agentic/*.py examples, and the 4B agent reads them in bulk: its median new tokens jump from ~2.4k to ~23k, with time and output skyrocketing as well, for no gain in accuracy.

Qwen3-4B across revisions. The CLI + Skill commit fans the cost distribution wide open, on the clone tier the agent reads the newly-shipped CLI source in bulk (~10× the new tokens), for no gain in match %. (repeat tokens stays flat: this setup uses no prompt caching.)

Sometimes, though, the Skill breaks correctness outright. Reading the traces shows how, for example for Qwen3-14B: adding the Skill drops its overall match rate from 67% (bare) to 43%, and on the simplest tasks the collapse is very visible: classify-sentiment goes from 100% on the clone variant to 0% with the Skill.

Qwen3-14B on classify-sentiment, by tier: clone (blue) holds at 100% across revisions, but the Skill variant (green) collapses to 0% at the CLI + Skill revision.

Looking at the traces, the model mistakes the CLI for a tool it can call directly (as in an agentic-harness tool, like web-search). The Skill is not an executable tool: it's documentation loaded into the agent's context, and the transformers CLI is only ever meant to be run from the shell (via bash); so this will not work.

Qwen3-14B reads the Skill and, in 39 of its 56 Skill runs, either emits a transformers(command="classify", ...) tool call (a tool that was never registered) or, finding nothing like it among its read/bash/edit/write tools, concludes it can't run a model and gives up. Either way, rather than fall back to the one-line pipeline(...) that scored 100% on the clone checkout, it declares the task impossible.

Qwen3-14B on classify-sentiment (Skill variant): it reasons that read/bash/edit/write can't run a model, and gives up.

This is exactly what we built the harness to catch: the same change that speeds the large models ends up breaking the small ones, which seemed a bit counterintuitive to us at first and something we'd likely have shipped as-is. The takeaway for maintainers: agent-facing APIs should be evaluated across model sizes, because a new affordance can reduce work for strong models while adding ambiguity for smaller ones. It also hints at a fix: rather than hand-write a Skill and check it after the fact, you could generate and validate one against the weaker models up front.

This is exactly what Upskill does: it turns a strong model's solution into a Skill only when it measurably helps the smaller ones.

The harness is one CLI, agent-eval. Install it, run a suite, fan it out across models × revisions on HF Jobs, and publish the report as a Hugging Face Space.

Trusted local use only. The harness runs a coding agent with bypassed permissions and executes code from whatever revision you point it at, and traces can contain prompts, output, and local paths. See SECURITY.md before pointing it at code you didn't write or sharing results.

The full, kept-current setup and usage instructions live in the README.

Checking the final answer tells you whether an agent can use your library. It doesn't tell you what it costs: the turns, tokens, errors, and the path it took to get there. This harness measures that, across the revisions and models you pick.

On transformers, it caught something we'd have shipped on faith: the CLI + Skill helps the largest open models and hurts the smallest ones. Worth knowing before merging!

It's profile-based, and designed to be adaptable: point it at your own library, define a few tasks and their expected answers, get the same report. Code and tasks are in the repo, traces are on the Hub. Let us know if you use it for your project!

This harness stands entirely on pi, Mario Zechner's coding-agent CLI: it drives every open-model run, and only needs an HF_TOKEN to serve a model, which is what made the open-model sweep practical at all.

Thanks to the model builders and inference providers behind the models we swept. Across the board they performed well above what the bare baseline would suggest.
