#9913. Burnt TOAST

Postgres at AI speed — deploy anywhere. Explore pgEdge Starfleet →

A financial firm hired me in 2010 to revise their Postgres cluster architecture. During my stint there, I learned a healthy respect for their event_log table. But perhaps “respect” is the wrong word here, as it was more of a deep loathing. This table, you see, was the canonical ledger of system events and consisted of several million rows.

The high row count wasn’t a problem by itself. We kept a tight visibility window and archived frequently. Unfortunately for us, one of the columns was an unconstrained TEXT type that commonly held a large blob of XML. Thus any fetch from this table was inordinately slow. Writing was equally painful. We went through great pains to shape the application itself to avoid touching it except when absolutely necessary. It was evil incarnate.

The performance of this table initially confused and enraged me—until I remembered about TOAST. Postgres likes to innocuously dub this backronym “The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique” but DBAs in the field maintain a love/hate relationship with the system. Whether that’s justified is a different question.

On the surface, it’s a way to store huge blocks of data elsewhere to keep tuples small and avoid exceeding the relatively petite 8KB data page size. Postgres creates a shadow table for the bulky content, splits it up into chunks, and stores a pointer in the original row. It’s an elegant solution to a pressing issue, but there are deep performance implications.

So let’s dig into precisely why DBAs secretly dread large text-based columns, shall we?

To really understand what happened in my event_log case, it’s good to reconstruct some semblance of it.

And then we can bootstrap the table with 100k rows. Just enough to make it annoying! The data column needs to be big, but not absolutely gigantic. Let’s start with up to 1000 data points:

Great! Now where did all of that data go? If you thought, “Into the event_log table of course!” you’re wrong. Instead, Postgres helpfully created a TOAST table for most of it. Let’s check the pg_class catalog for the other objects:

That’s three objects for the price of one: the original table, a toast table, and a toast table index. This doesn’t always happen, but if your table has a text-like column without a maximum length, it probably did. In this case, it’s because an unbounded JSON column can contain anything, so Postgres preemptively initialized a TOAST table to store the “anything”.

What goes in is a bit more subtle, and is where the trouble starts brewing.

There’s a kind of inherent hierarchy that determines how data gets managed. The typstorage column in the pg_type catalog explains how this works for each type Postgres understands. There are four valid storage methods:

PLAIN (p): The value stays inline and uncompressed. This is the default for fixed-width types like INT and TIMESTAMPTZ.

MAIN (m): Compression is allowed, with TOAST only as the last resort. The default for NUMERIC.

EXTERNAL (e): TOAST is allowed, but compression is not.

EXTENDED (x): Anything is fair game. This is the default for TEXT, BYTEA, JSONB, and most other variable-length types.

Postgres imposes a loop on all text-based column types in a tuple that it applies until the entire row is under the standard 8KB page threshold (minus overhead). It looks something like this:

Being the default for JSON, all of our data follows the rules for EXTENDED. We can see it in action by checking a few rows:

The toast_tuple_target storage setting tells Postgres when to toast column contents. The default is around 2KB of compressed data, and anything after that is moved into TOAST automatically. The example above has a row that compresses right under that limit, and as a result, never gets moved.

If we examine page 57 specifically, this becomes even more clear:

The tuple size of the rows that didn’t get toasted is much larger than those that did. That’s thanks to a pointer replacing the toasted values. And that’s not all. Toasted data is also broken into chunks. Every toasted value gets broken into 1996-byte blocks and stored in sequential order as rows in the toast table.

Any toasted value implies at least one fetch from the toast table. That’s a read on the toast index and a read on the toast table itself per chunk.

Chunks must be re-assembled. That’s extra memory usage and can be significant depending on chunk count.

Compressed data must also be decompressed. That’s both memory and CPU overhead.

The intuitive read of this is that TOAST is always worse. But is it?

Let’s run an experiment! We already have a table where some of the data is toasted. What happens if we force Postgres to select all of it?

This requires some setup. To begin, we create a non-toasted table by setting the event_data column to use MAIN storage. That allows it to be compressed, but not toasted unless the full tuple exceeds a Postgres page size. Like so:

Then we can directly compare the costs of pulling out field 999 from the data:

Take a look at that! Shared buffers really saved our bacon on this one. Total buffer reads on the toasted column required 288127 total reads versus 40754 for the non-toasted version. Conversely, the toasted table is much smaller:

While Postgres can read through the heap faster, it then has to spend a lot of time seeking through the toast table. This size difference translates to some non-intuitive behavior. For instance, most interactions with the toasted table are actually much faster. Consider counting all rows:

That’s 26ms vs 91ms. Or jumping through offsets:

Any time Postgres has to deal directly with the heap, performance suffers immensely. Toast pointers can act as an optimization, particularly when not interacting with the toasted column because they make each row on the heap much smaller.

This one kind of blew my mind. It turns out that the problem with the event_log table wasn’t necessarily the TOAST system, but the event_data column itself. It turns out there’s a way to fix that.

Back then, “fixing that” meant to split the table. Our toy example is a mere 100k rows, but the real one was several million and the heap alone was over 1GB. Including TOAST on those huge XML blobs brought the total table size to over 20GB.

When an application is full of SELECT * and is repeatedly looking up and decoding toasted data, it can eventually take a toll. Even if we ignore the disk IO, that’s a lot of extra network bandwidth. “Just specify the column names!” you might say, and I agree. If only it were that easy to modify ORM-generated queries and five years of accumulated hand-written ones.

What do we gain from this? For one, we no longer need to carry around the TOAST pointers in the main application table. Secondly, since this column was a mix of toasted and non-toasted values due to the toast_tuple_target cutoff, even non-toasted values have been relocated. We can see this in the new table heap sizes:

All operations will now be substantially faster simply because page density is now guaranteed to be higher. More rows fit on each page, and there are fewer pages required to represent the primary core of the table. The entire heap is now 5MB rather than 47MB, a saving of over 9x. If it’s at all possible to relocate large columns to an optional JOIN in a high-performance system, it may be worth taking a second look.

If you think we could have achieved a similar effect by setting toast_tuple_target arbitrarily low, think again. The TOAST system won’t even activate if a row value is shorter than TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD, a compiled value that acts as a hard minimum. Values below this won’t even be considered for toasting. What can I say? Postgres is a picky eater.

The obvious objection is that applications now need a join. Well, the Postgres planner has you covered:

The trick is the LEFT JOIN, making the event data optional even though we know every row has a value there. Queries that don’t specify the column will prune the JOIN and everyone is happy.

As of Postgres 14, it’s even possible to choose the compression type. Stick with the venerable built-in pglz, or use lz4 if it’s been compiled into your binaries. The default for the entire server comes from default_toast_compression:

Or it can be set using the COMPRESSION decorator during CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE.

One interesting note about the compression types is that pglz is somewhat quirky. It skips values under 32 bytes, demands at least 25% savings, and gives up entirely if it finds nothing to compress in the first 1KB. The last rule is kind of odd to see in action:

There are also some associated performance implications. Consider:

When dealing with 100k rows of 10k compressed values, lz4 is a bit slower decompressing by about 20% in this case, but is over 30 times faster at compression. That’s absolutely staggering.

Look, we all want to play the blame game. I always blamed the TOAST system for how badly our application’s event_log table performed. Every time someone complained. Any occasion when a badly written query made it through the application and touched the table in a way that apparently enraged it and caused every page load to quadruple or time out entirely. In my head, TOAST was at fault.

Ironically, it was TOAST’s fault in a way, because it’s not aggressive enough. Think about it. Postgres needs TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD to avoid activating the expensive machinery that deconstructs, compresses, and moves data to an external table. But imagine how things could look if anything could be offloaded arbitrarily. Unfortunately there’s no option for that. Out of PLAIN, MAIN, EXTENDED, and EXTERNAL, none cover the case for “move anything over 100 bytes and also compress it if it’s over 2k.” Though there’s an argument for using EXTERNAL on medium-sized but “large-ish” columns: we gain the benefit of a smaller heap, and data less than 1kb doesn’t tend to compress well anyway.

Instead, we have to compromise our schema design and introduce an extra join for parts of the application that actually interact with the bulky column. Views sidestep this to an extent, but it’s something of an ugly hack compared to leaving the table intact. We also can’t leverage this maneuver every single time a big column shows up, or our schema would end up a horrifying mess. Not all columns are “optional” enough to banish.

What TOAST provides is a suitable middle-ground. For the cost of a pointer, we get to essentially forget a huge block of text exists in the table at all. The heap is happier and we’re none the wiser. Compression speeds are also dramatically faster for those who switch to lz4.

So don’t be afraid of Postgres TOAST; it’s the best kind there is.

#9912. Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills

Nathan Hamiel outlines potential SecOps horror in the AI midst, as core technical capabilities go the way of reading an atlas or remembering phone numbers.

Black Hat India — Bengaluru — The use of AI as a tool to enhance cybersecurity operations is emerging as a double-edged knife for security professionals. While it can make them more capable, it could also spell the demise of the very skills they need to use it effectively.

That's the concern of Nathan Hamiel, senior director of research at Kudelski Security, who has made a case for how evolving technology can erode technical skills since well before the generative AI boom. Now, that concern is getting much louder.

Speaking to Dark Reading recently, he says he began noticing the problem around 2005 and 2006, when he encountered cybersecurity professionals who lacked a firm grasp of the fundamentals of their work. At that time, he warned about the dangers of relying too heavily on various types of technical tools, declaring to cybersecurity professionals that "your tools are killing you," and warning that practitioners are moving away from being "hands-on" operators who investigate problems directly, and toward "hands-off" monitors who oversee results presented through tools, interfaces, and dashboards.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

It's a shift that's being exacerbated now by AI-driven automation, he says, and organizations need to move quickly to optimize the use of AI without the expense of cybersecurity skill-building.

While automation can simplify complex tasks and allow professionals to accomplish more, it can also distance them from the underlying problems they are trying to solve. Without a solid understanding of the fundamentals, practitioners may struggle to recognize when a tool produces an incorrect result or when its findings require further investigation, Hamiel says.

"We need to keep these skills and not let them degrade because those skills are important to making the tools work in the best way possible," he tells Dark Reading from this week's Black Hat India conference, where he's giving a keynote entitled "The Death of Skills and the Persistence of Problems."

"What AI adds to somebody with knowledge and experience is some additional capabilities," Hamiel elaborates. "A domain expert wielding AI is going to be able to gain benefits from using that tool that a novice with no domain experience isn't going to be able to get."

This distinction is becoming increasingly important as AI becomes more deeply integrated into cybersecurity workflows. It also raises questions about how the industry will develop its next generation of experts if automation removes some of the hands-on tasks that junior professionals traditionally learn.

Related:Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

The current discussion around AI often falls into extremes, Hamiel says. Some predict that the technology can go a long way toward solving major problems facing not only cybersecurity but also humanity, while others warn that it will bring the industry — and some even the world — to an end.

"You have the doomers," he says, "and you have people who say this is a big nothingburger. The truth is somewhere in the middle."

For Hamiel, understanding AI's impact requires separating what the technology can demonstrate in a controlled environment from what it can reliably accomplish in the real world. Impressive capabilities do not necessarily translate into the wholesale replacement of jobs or the disappearance of entire industries, he says.

The same distinction applies to cybersecurity, Hamiel says. Although AI can help identify vulnerabilities, generate code and support security investigations, those capabilities do not mean that the complex problems facing security teams have suddenly become easy to solve.

In fact, some recent incidents described as "rogue" AI activity — such as OpenAI models autonomously hacking the Hugging Face framework, among others — may reveal a more familiar and persistent cybersecurity problem: organizations failing to address basic security weaknesses.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"If you read some of the incident reports, these are organizations that weren't exercising basic security hygiene," Hamiel says.

In these cases, he argues, the weaknesses were already there, waiting to be discovered. "This wasn't just low-hanging fruit; this was fruit lying on the ground where anybody who looked for it would have found it," he says.

Rather than signaling an impending cybersecurity apocalypse, such incidents could prompt what Hamiel calls a "cybersecurity correction."

"It's not that there is this huge apocalypse happening; it's that many people weren't doing the right thing for a very long time," he explains.

In other words, AI may make it easier to discover and exploit existing weaknesses, exposing the consequences of inadequate security practices. The challenge for organizations is not simply to adopt new tools but to address the underlying problems those tools bring to light.

Indeed, the potential erosion of technical skills is not a problem that began with generative AI. Hamiel sees it as part of a longer trend in which technology increasingly mediates the relationship between professionals and the problems they are responsible for solving.

Hamiel's concern reflects what is often called the irony of automation: As systems take on more responsibility, the humans overseeing them can lose opportunities to practice the skills needed when those systems fail.

The consequences could extend beyond the skills of today's practitioners to the way the cybersecurity industry develops future experts, he says, especially in how lower-level work that AI can eliminate helps helping junior professionals learn.

Tasks that might appear repetitive or straightforward can provide essential experience, allowing new practitioners to understand how systems work before progressing to more complex investigations. "If you automate that, there isn't room for them to learn," Hamiel warns.

This creates a potential long-term problem for employers. AI may allow teams to complete certain tasks more efficiently today, but organizations still need experienced professionals who can investigate unfamiliar problems, evaluate automated findings, and respond when systems behave unexpectedly.

For cybersecurity pros to use generative AI effectively, then, it's simply a matter of applying it to tasks where it offers meaningful benefits while remaining aware of the skills that might be weakened if pros rely too much on these tools to do their jobs effectively.

"The goal here is to maximize the benefits and minimize the drawbacks," Hamiel says, something that is true for the use of any technology. "That's the framing that should be placed around this," he says.

Thus, the only way that organizations can adopt AI without losing essential cybersecurity expertise is to "apply them to the right types of activities," he says.

For cybersecurity pros, this means using generative AI for tasks such as threat hunting and threat intelligence, where preliminary analysis can help professionals work through information more efficiently, Hamiel notes. AI-powered penetration-testing tools are another area of promising development, extending beyond traditional vulnerability scanning to perform more complex tasks, he says.

Ultimately, the question is not whether AI will change cybersecurity, Hamiel says. That genie is most certainly already out of that bottle. Ultimately, the real challenge is ensuring that the industry does not become so dependent on increasingly capable tools that it loses the human expertise required to use them effectively, he says.

"Skills and expertise make your AI use more effective," Hamiel concludes. "If you have two professionals, and both use AI, the one with more knowledge of the task is going to make better use of the AI."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9911. Featuring Every Eval Ever Results on Hugging Face Model Pages

Every Eval Ever (EEE) and Hugging Face Community Evals are now intercompatible. We enable cross-posting and interpreting evaluation results, while linking to open models, leaderboards, and a unified standardized metadata store.

EEE launched in February 2026 as a project of the EvalEval Coalition, the first cross-institutional effort to improve how AI evaluation results get reported by both first and third party evaluators. Hugging Face launched Community Evals in February 2026 to decentralize how benchmark scores get reported on the Hub. Combined, they patch gaps in how users, researchers, and policymakers trust, understand, and choose evaluations and models.

Evaluation results are how we measure model capabilities, compare models against each other, and reason about safety and governance, and yet they are scattered and hard to compare. They live in papers, leaderboards, blog posts, and harness logs, among others, each in its own format. The same model on the same benchmark often returns different scores depending on who ran it and how; LLaMA 65B, for one, has been reported at both 63.7 and 48.8 on MMLU. These gaps can arise from evaluation settings that we found are commonly unreported.

EEE is our fix for the reporting side. It's one JSON schema for an evaluation result that records:

The schema was built with feedback from researchers and policy researchers, and it takes in results from any source, so harness logs, leaderboard scrapes, and paper numbers all end up in the same shape. The GitHub repository has the converters, examples, and a contributor guide. Since launching, the datastore on Hugging Face has grown to around 229,000 evaluation results across more than 22,000 models and 2,200 benchmarks, pulled from 31 different reporting formats. Reproducing just those runs from scratch would cost somewhere in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, which is a reasonable argument for not letting the data scatter once someone has paid to generate it.

Learn more about the schema and how to contribute here.

Now, it comes with better integration and attribution. Contributors can now send EEE results to Hugging Face Community Evals. We built a converter that takes your EEE records and writes the small YAML files Hugging Face expects, so you don't have to keep the same result in two formats by hand.

This is new functionality for everyone who reports or reads evaluations, not only existing EEE contributors. First-party evaluators reporting on their own models and third-party evaluators reporting on someone else's can both submit to Community Evals and to EEE, and anyone browsing the Hub gets results that trace back to a full record. When you submit your data through your organization's official Hugging Face account, your results show up with a verified checkmark on EvalEval, a signal to readers that the numbers come straight from the source. The rest of this post walks through what Community Evals are and what the converter does.

Hugging Face Community Evals has two sides.

A benchmark lives in a dataset repo that registers itself by adding an eval.yaml. Once registered, that dataset page collects and displays a leaderboard of every score reported against it across the Hub. The list of official benchmarks grows over time.

A model's scores live in .eval_results/*.yaml inside the model repo. They show up on the model card and feed into the matching benchmark leaderboard. Both the model author's own results and results submitted by anyone else through a pull request get aggregated, and each score carries a badge saying whether it was author-submitted, community-submitted, or independently verified. Anyone can add a score to any model by opening a PR with the right YAML file, and the model author can close PRs or hide results on their own repo.

Here is what one of these leaderboards looks like:

Community Evals Leaderboard for Humanity's Last Exam on the Hub

This is where EEE and Community Evals fit together. When you send a result to both, two things happen: First, your score appears on the Hugging Face model page and gets pulled into the benchmark's leaderboard. And second, it carries a source badge that links straight back to the full EEE record, where the generation config, the harness version, the reproducibility notes, and any instance-level data live.

An Evaluation (MMLU-Pro) from EEE Datastore (a) cross-linked at the file level to a Hugging Face model card (b). The Source EvalEval badge links to the full JSON record.

The two destinations do different jobs toward the same goal. Hugging Face puts your result where people look at models, with a link back to the source. EEE keeps the full structured record that makes the result interpretable, and powers Eval Cards on top of it. Send your data to both and the same evaluation ends up visible and legible at once, which is the point of reporting one at all.

You can see that cross-compatibility below. The same GPQA scores that surface on the model card above also render in Eval Cards, which composes the EEE run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record. Same evaluation, a different surface:

Hugging Face stores eval scores in the model repo as a YAML under .eval_results/. The required fields are just the benchmark dataset, the task, and the value. The source block is the part that creates the backlink to EEE.

The converter fills this in from your existing records. It maps source_data.hf_repo to dataset.id, evaluation_name to task_id, score_details.score to value, and evaluation_timestamp to date, then drops in the datastore object URL as the source link to the per-record EEE JSON. It currently handles four of the official benchmarks: MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE, and GSM8K.

The converter does more than reshape fields. You point it at one EEE datastore collection and it downloads that collection along with the records it references, checks the object hashes, and finds the scores that map to a supported benchmark. Before it writes anything live it audits what already exists: it reads every .eval_results YAML on the model's main branch and in open PRs, and compares by dataset and task rather than by filename. If a score is already there it is marked already_present, if a different score is there it is flagged as a score_conflict, and if the model repo doesn't resolve on the Hub it is marked missing_hf_model. Everything else is marked ready.

Nothing gets pushed without your sign-off. The tool writes local YAML previews and a review file you can inspect, shows a report of what is ready and what needs attention, and only opens PRs after you type OPEN PRS and enter a commit message. Reruns reuse the cached results for a collection unless you pass --force.

The converter's review step. Excluded entries (here, models with no matching Hub repo) are listed with their EEE source URLs, and the ready PRs wait on an explicit OPEN PRS confirmation.

Submit your full records to the EEE datastore.

Utilizing EEE requires only one additional step, which the converter largely automates. The community eval converter tool can be found in the GitHub repository. To process a collection, execute the following:

Review the previews and the report it generates, then type OPEN PRS when you're ready to submit. Full documentation for the schema, CLI, and converters is at evalevalai.com/every_eval_ever/hf-community-evals.

#9909. Palantir CEO says it's pioneering an antiwar movement – while happily accepting defense dollars

Alex Karp casts military software as a force for peace while declaring a moral imperative to dominate the market

Alex Karp, CEO of US spy-tech company Palantir, used this week's historic US midterm election results to claim an unlikely mantle for a military software supplier: pioneer of an antiwar movement.

Palantir's Q3 revenue rose 96 percent year-on-year to $2.31 billion, although its shares fell 8 percent following the results, which it reported on Tuesday as US voters were delivering a resounding defeat for Republicans in the voting booth. For Karp, the figures represented "the reality that this moment has become a real focal point of understanding" and might help explain "what is happening in our society."

From the CEO's perspective, they not only reflected the company's financial performance, but also its overall "mission."

"That mission reason is we support your alpha [above average performance], we support your sovereignty. We support the war fighter. We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money. But we believe we have a moral imperative to be the dominant player in our industry," he told investors.

For Karp-watchers, this is familiar self-serving shtick: turn Palantir's work for military and intelligence customers into a moral crusade, and goad its critics along the way.

"There's this larger question of what does it mean to have a business that was built around what we believed and believe now is the most important mission in the world, supporting our war fighters, [and] bringing them home," he said.

None of this stops him presenting Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement," he wrote in his shareholder letter.

He expanded on the point during the Q3 earnings call. "Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that, in fact, it's not worth going to war and also to create social cohesion because we're going to bring back our troops healthier, safer, undamaged and that makes our society much more effective," he said.

That antiwar pitch sits awkwardly alongside Karp's $1 million donation in December 2024 to MAGA Inc., the super PAC supporting Donald Trump. Trump subsequently launched a US military operation in Venezuela and went to war with Iran, repeatedly promising the latter conflict would be short-lived as it dragged on. Karp did not address either topic on the call.

Elsewhere, Karp claimed that Palantir "built products that would protect civil liberties and stop terrorism. If you don't stop terrorism, you're going to get a radical fringe on the right. If you stop terrorism without rights, none of us wants that."

That civil liberties pitch also invites scrutiny of Palantir's longstanding relationship with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), whose treatment of people it targets and detains has drawn criticism from US judges.

Karp seems to enjoy the circus of controversy he and his colleagues have created. He also offered investors this insight: "The future is becoming the present and the present is now." Whatever that future holds, he seems confident Palantir has a moral imperative to invoice it. ®

#9907. Why Specialization Is Inevitable

Those who follow Dharma AI already know that we view specialization as one of the defining principles of effective AI systems, shaping everything from cost and performance to reliability and sovereignty. Few papers have articulated that case as rigorously as the 2026 work by Goldfeder, Wyder, LeCun, and Shwartz-Ziv.

In this article, we explore and interpret ideas from AI Must Embrace Specialization via Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (Goldfeder, Wyder, LeCun, & Shwartz-Ziv, 2026). The paper's convergence case — spanning optimization theory, biology, organizational economics, and machine learning — provides both the evidential structure and the intellectual foundation for the discussion that follows. The framing, organization, and editorial synthesis presented here are Dharma's.

The conventional expectation is reasonable: as AI systems grow more capable, they should also grow more general. Greater capability and broader applicability seem like natural companions — more resources, better methods, and expanded training should produce systems that approach more tasks with increasing confidence.

The pattern that actually appears is different. The systems that achieve the most significant results in any given domain tend to be the ones most narrowly focused on it. The breakthrough in protein structure prediction came from a system engineered for a single scientific task. The historical milestones of AI, examined closely, reflect intense domain targeting rather than expanding generality.

This pattern recurs. It recurs across domains, across decades, across architectural choices that have almost nothing in common. A pattern this consistent suggests a common cause — one that does not originate inside AI research at all.

In 1997, Wolpert and Macready proved something that rarely surfaces in discussions of AI architecture: no single, general-purpose optimization algorithm outperforms all others across all possible problems (Wolpert & Macready, 1997). The proof is mathematical, not philosophical. Averaged across every conceivable problem a learner might face, every algorithm performs equally well — and equally poorly. An algorithm that gains on one distribution of problems necessarily concedes on others. The performance is redistributed, not multiplied.

The practical implication is direct: “an algorithm wins by being a good fit for the target problem” (Goldfeder et al., 2026). The theorem does not say generality is impossible — it says generality is not a performance advantage. The consistent structural path to outperformance is concentration: trading breadth for fit.

This becomes sharper when finite resources enter the picture. Any real system operates under constraints — finite compute, finite data, finite development time. Given finite energy, an approach that directs available resources toward learning a finite set of tasks will outperform one that distributes those same resources across an unlimited range. The arithmetic is unforgiving: as the task set expands without bound, the resources available per task shrink toward zero. Universal coverage and meaningful performance are, under finite resources, in direct tension.

The conclusion the theorem points toward is not that generality is bad. It is narrower and more operational than that: as the paper states, "universal generality is a theoretical concept, but in practical terms it is a myth" (Goldfeder et al., 2026). What survives contact with real constraints is not the system that tries to do everything — it is the system that fits its target.

The mathematics establishes this as a prediction, not a preference. Whether that prediction holds in the world beyond optimization theory is a different question.

Two other domains arrived at the same prediction before optimization theory gave it a name.

As the paper describes the biological case: every performance gain in one niche comes at a cost elsewhere. A generalist carries traits suited to many environments but optimal for none — competence spread too thin to dominate any particular condition. There are no performance gains without trade-offs; the resources invested in one capability are unavailable for another. Selection favors designs matched to local conditions over those optimized for uniform coverage across all possible environments. The organisms that survive to reproduce are not the most generally capable — they are the most specifically matched. The result, accumulated over evolutionary timescales, is not generalists dominating — it is specialists filling niches. As the paper states: "Specialization is not an accident of biology; it is a predictable consequence of limited resources, competing objectives, and environments that reward performance on a small subset of evolutionarily relevant challenges" (Goldfeder et al., 2026).

Competitive markets follow the same dynamic through different means. Organizations and strategies that fail to meet performance thresholds are eliminated — not through extinction, but through exit, defunding, and replacement by better-matched alternatives. Competition acts as a selection mechanism: it amplifies effective strategies and eliminates ineffective ones. The mechanism has nothing in common with biological selection — no inheritance, no mutation, no evolutionary timescale. The unit of selection is not the organism but the organization, the product, the strategy. Yet the structural pressure is the same: finite resources, performance requirements, and the systematic removal of entities too broadly distributed to excel where it counts. Concentrated capacity outcompetes distributed capacity when performance standards are clear and consistent.

Evolution and markets operate through entirely different mechanisms — different timescales, different units of selection, different inheritance mechanisms. Yet both produce the same outcome under resource pressure: fit over breadth. The theorem predicts this. Biology and markets arrive at it independently. When a third domain arrives at the same finding through different means entirely, the pattern ceases to look like a theorem and begins to look like something more general about how constrained systems behave.

The same pattern has emerged inside machine learning — not derived from optimization theory, but arrived at through the accumulated experience of building systems and watching what improves them.

The clearest form is negative transfer: a measurable degradation that occurs when a system trained on multiple tasks suffers because those tasks compete rather than cooperate (Ruder, 2017). When tasks share structure, training together helps. But when tasks compete for representational capacity, or impose conflicting gradients during training, performance on individual tasks falls below what a dedicated system would achieve. The gain from breadth becomes a cost to depth. It is a documented consequence of dividing finite capacity across tasks that pull against each other. The specialist, facing no such competition, does not pay this cost.

The architecture of frontier models offers a different form of evidence. Mixture-of-experts systems achieve their breadth not through uniform generality across all parameters, but by routing each input to a specialized subset of the network — activating different experts for different tasks. The paper's authors read this as a structural concession: a system designed to be general achieving its results by recovering specialization internally. This is an argued interpretation, not a demonstrated theorem — these architectures were designed for computational efficiency, and what they imply about generality's limits is a reasonable inference rather than a stated intent. But it is a notable one: the most capable general-purpose systems reach their performance by doing internally what specialist systems do by design.

The clearest historical example follows the same logic. AlphaFold achieved a step change in protein structure prediction by targeting that specific task with task-specific architecture and training choices (Jumper et al., 2021). Its gains came from narrower focus, not broader coverage. The paper uses AlphaFold as an archetypal case — not as evidence that all specialized systems achieve equivalent gains, but as an unusually clear illustration of the mechanism. That mechanism has appeared repeatedly: the history of AI milestones, the paper notes, frequently reflects intense domain targeting rather than broad competence, even when the results look like demonstrations of general intelligence.

Three distinct places. Three different mechanisms. The same finding.

The picture would be incomplete without addressing one of AI research's most cited observations. Sutton's Bitter Lesson holds that methods relying on domain knowledge are consistently outperformed by methods that scale computation (Sutton, 2019). On its face, this appears to complicate the case for specialization: if scale and generality win, perhaps specialization is only a useful heuristic under resource constraints that will ease as compute becomes cheaper.

The objection rests on a conflation between two distinct concepts. Domain knowledge refers to hand-coded features, engineered priors, and rules designed to give a system insight into a particular area. The Bitter Lesson targets this — and it is correct to do so. Systems that encode explicit domain knowledge have been consistently outperformed as scale increases.

Domain specialization is different: the decision to direct a system's resources, architecture, and training toward a bounded set of tasks rather than distributing them broadly. This is not the encoding of knowledge about a domain. It is a decision about scope.

The paper draws the distinction precisely:

"The diminishing usefulness of domain knowledge is distinct from the usefulness of domain specialization. As scaling progresses, we will need to know less about proteins to build a system that does protein folding; however, such a system still benefits from focusing specifically on proteins." (Goldfeder et al., 2026)

Scaling changes what systems can learn from data. It does not change whether concentrating resources on a finite task set outperforms distributing them across an unlimited range. The Bitter Lesson and the specialization argument operate on different dimensions — one describes how knowledge should be acquired, the other describes what a system should be pointed at. Both can be true simultaneously. Scaling changes the mechanisms by which systems learn; it does not dissolve the constraint that makes fit more valuable than breadth.

Across four analytical traditions, the same pattern emerged through different paths. This is not a coincidence that demands explanation. It is the evidence.

When finite resources meet selection pressure — in an optimization problem, an ecosystem, a market, or a training run — fit consistently beats breadth. The specific mechanisms differ. The timescales differ. The units of selection differ. But the structural dynamic is the same, and it produces the same result.

The theorem does not cause this pattern in biology. Biology does not cause it in markets. Neither causes it in machine learning. They all face the same underlying constraint: performance under scarcity requires concentration. What the theorem establishes mathematically, evolutionary history confirms empirically, competitive markets demonstrate institutionally, and machine learning rediscovers architecturally.

Specialization is not a preference. It is what emerges when finite resources meet the requirement to perform.

If you're evaluating how domain focus affects AI performance in your organization — or building the case internally for a specialization strategy — we'd like to hear about your context. Get in touch with Dharma AI.

Forister, M.L., Novotny, V., Panorska, A.K., Baje, L., Basset, Y., Butterill, P.T., & Dyer, L.A. (2012). Global distribution of diet breadth in insect herbivores. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(2), 418–423.

Futuyma, D.J. & Moreno, G. (1988). The evolution of ecological specialization. Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics, 19, 207–233.

Hannan, M.T. & Freeman, J. (1977). The population ecology of organizations. American Journal of Sociology, 82(5), 929–964.

Loasby, B.J. (1983). Knowledge, learning and the firm. As cited in Goldfeder et al. (2026).

Ruder, S. (2017). An overview of multi-task learning in deep neural networks. arXiv:1706.05098.

Fedus, W., Zoph, B., & Shazeer, N. (2022). Switch transformers: Scaling to trillion parameter models with simple and efficient sparsity. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 23(120), 1–39.

Where the No Free Lunch theorem establishes why specialization is structurally predicted, this piece examines the evidence that it outperforms in practice — and why it remains underweighted in most AI procurement decisions.

I would add that in the era of AI Agents, deploying a new hyperspecialized agent with a very narrow domain and less prompts/context, would lead to less hallucinations and less token comsuption. It's cheap and convenient, so is the most probable path in my opinion.

The top line thesis — specialization beats generality — is (forgive me) something of a PGIO (penetrating glimpse into the obvious). I do appreciate the distinction between domain knowledge and domain specialization. They're not the same axis, and conflating them is a common mistake. Regretably, the authors stop right where things get interesting. Domain knowledge's value-add is described as diminishing as scale increases, with no stated floor. Specialization's value-add is described as persisting; not growing, just not eroding the way knowledge does. That's a decline running against a flat line, not two things moving in the same direction at different speeds. The authors never say where that decline runs out, or when investing further in expert content stops paying off — compared to just narrowing scope. A distinction this precise about what specialization is deserves precision about when to stop chasing knowledge and start chasing focus. How much is enough? 10K hours worth (a la Malcolm Gladwell)?

Great point, and I agree that this is where the discussion becomes most interesting.

It is not possible to say where the decline bottoms out, since neural networks learn representations through superposition rather than assigning individual neurons or subnetworks to specific domains. In other words, it is not possible to isolate parts of the network and claim that they are responsible for domain X or domain Y, as these domains are encoded through overlapping representations. What we can affirm is that it depends on the relationship between breadth of domains in the knowledge base and the number of parameters of the model (the greater the parameters, the greater the capacity to retain knowledge). To answer this question, we would need some way of measuring the amount of domain knowledge contained in the training data, as well as the degree of overlap between those domains in the latent space learned by a highly non-linear neural network. I believe this question is currently intractable.

Regarding the point at which investing in specialized content ceases to pay off, I believe that this only happens when the objective is to build a genuinely more general-purpose model. If the goal is to use the available resources (parameters) to provide shallow responses across a broad range of topics, then it makes more sense to train on a dataset with broad coverage but relatively little depth in each domain. On the other hand, if the objective is to build a model that solves a finite and relatively small set of tasks, more specialized data will always be the better choice. Naturally, as you increase the size of that task set, you eventually return to the first scenario of wanting a general-purpose model.

The same reasoning applies to the question of when we should pursue greater focus: whenever the scope of the application is itself focused. It is fundamentally a design choice. If you are training a model for open-ended tasks that may receive any type of input, it is better to have a model that responds superficially across many topics than one that responds deeply to only a few. Conversely, if the application has a well-defined scope, it will always be better to train a model specialized for that scope, making more efficient use of its resources instead of spending them on knowledge that will never be required.

That said, these are very relevant questions, and we hope to address at least part of them through mechanistic interpretability, which is one of the research areas within our R&D efforts. The techniques in this field allow us to observe internal circuits within models, sparsely used neurons, neurons that activate under specific conditions, and other internal mechanisms. This may help us better understand how models work internally and answer some of your questions more directly.

#9905. Hey, Siri: Plug into my app like you said you'd do way back in 2024

More than two years after promising it, Apple lets developers test Siri AI app integration

As of Tuesday, developers can explore expanded Siri AI integration for their Apple platform apps through beta releases of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. Next spring, nearly three years after announcing plans for deeper third-party Siri integration, Apple expects to begin accepting App Store submissions using the new capabilities.

"This developer beta offers a sneak peek at Siri AI app intents for developers," Apple said in a developer news post. "With this early Developer Preview, your app can work directly with Siri AI, giving you a first look at new ways to reach and serve your customers."

Anything is likely to be an improvement. Apple's Siri, a voice-activated assistant service, dates back to 2011 and gained limited third-party app access in 2016. In 2024, it became an interface for interacting with Apple Intelligence, its suite of generative AI features.

Apple Intelligence has not been very intelligent – several advertised Siri capabilities were delayed, so much so that Apple was sued in 2025 over allegations of misleading marketing. After a shakeup of Apple's machine learning group in December 2025, Siri and Apple Intelligence received a makeover at Apple's Worldwide Developers Conference in June.

"Before this year, Siri was a timer with a voice," said Roberto Gutierrez, Apple platforms staff engineer at a media company and author of the e-book On-Device Intelligence, in an email to The Register. "Weather, alarms, calls. Anything past that was a coin toss.

"On the developer side, SiriKit covered a handful of domains and Shortcuts only worked if users memorized the phrase. Siri AI is the first version that understands context and can chain actions across apps. That's a real change."

There is a catch, however, Gutierrez observed. Siri AI is available in a limited number of languages and regions. Support for Traditional Chinese is expected by the end of 2026, and EU availability remains a matter of negotiation – Siri AI is unavailable on iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS in the bloc as Apple works through interoperability concerns under Europe's Digital Markets Act.

"Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward," the company said last month without committing to any concessions.

Gutierrez said that he expects opening Siri to third-party developers will be useful to some extent.

"Siri can only do what apps expose through App Intents, and SiriKit is on its way out," he said. "If your app's main actions aren't exposed, the new Siri can't see you. The bigger shift is letting Claude, Gemini and others plug in. Developers already choose between three options for every AI feature: Apple's system model, an open model through MLX, or a cloud API. Siri is heading the same way. It doesn't need to be the smartest model. It needs to be the best router. That's the right call."

Apple has made choosing between those three options more difficult by failing to publish benchmarks that show how its Foundation Models compare with open-weight alternatives.

The biz has published measurements of how its third-generation Foundation Models compare to their 2025 predecessors. But the company's commitment – to "[share] more details on our latest foundation models, including updated evaluations and benchmarks, in a technical report later this summer" – remains unfulfilled so far as we're aware.

Gutierrez ran his own benchmarks to compare Apple's iOS system model (FM system, ~3B) to several open-weight models that are suitable for use on-device.

"On an A17 Pro iPhone running iOS 26, I tested Apple's system model against Qwen3 1.7B and 4B, Llama 3.2 3B and Gemma 3 4B on a structured-output task," he said. "Speed: Apple's model ran at about 149 tok/s, roughly 3x the fastest open model (Qwen3 1.7B, about 46)."

Quality, he said, was a tie, with every model passing five typed checks. But memory, he said, was where Apple's models had an advantage.

"The system model's weights live outside your app's memory budget," he explained. "My app peaked at 12 MB during inference. An open 4B model costs 2.4-2.7 GB, and a 2.4 GB model plus your app plus a WebView is a crash report. So yes, it's competitive, and on iPhone it's the default I'd recommend. If you want your own model, Qwen3 1.7B is the one."

But Gutierrez urged Apple to publish proper competitive benchmarks. "Their numbers compare against their own previous models," he said. "Developers aren't choosing between Apple 2025 and Apple 2026. We're choosing between Apple, Qwen and a cloud API. I had to build my own harness to answer a question Apple could settle with one table."

The absence of competitive model metrics is not the only gap. Apple has also failed to accommodate web apps.

"Web apps are locked out," said Gutierrez. "Foundation Models is a Swift API (and now Python). No JavaScript, no WebKit. A PWA's only option is to ship its own model into the browser and pay the full memory bill inside a WebView."

And bringing your own model may pose performance problems. "On an A17 Pro iPhone, the 3-4B open models pushed the phone into 'fair' thermal state and dropped to 12-24 tok/s," he said. "In practice, your own model on iPhone means ~2B or smaller."

With Siri AI unavailable on iPhones, iPads, and Apple Watches in the EU (and its rollout in mainland China subject to regulatory requirements), developers may need a fallback for global apps to handle regional restrictions. Apple's Private Cloud Compute offers eligible developers access to Foundation Models, Gutierrez observed, though it requires membership in the App Store Small Business Program, fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads across their apps, and the necessary entitlement. ®

#9904. ScarfBench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Enterprise Java Framework Migration

Modernizing enterprise applications is one of the largest and most expensive software engineering activities organizations undertake. Teams migrate applications across frameworks to improve maintainability, cloud readiness, developer productivity, and access to modern capabilities.

Recent advances in coding agents have sparked excitement around AI-assisted modernization. But an important question remains:

Can AI agents reliably modernize real-world enterprise applications?

Existing software engineering benchmarks have demonstrated impressive progress in bug fixing and code generation, but framework migration presents a fundamentally different challenge. Success requires not only translating code, but also preserving behavior, adapting build systems, and navigating runtime dependencies.

To address this gap, we introduce ScarfBench (Self-Contained Application Refactoring Benchmark), an open benchmark for evaluating AI agents on cross-framework migration tasks in Enterprise Java.

ScarfBench focuses on migrations across three major Java ecosystems:

Unlike traditional benchmarks that compare generated code against reference implementations, ScarfBench evaluates whether migrated applications actually build, deploy, and preserve behavior.

Framework migration is much more than replacing annotations.

A simple repository migration can require changes across dependency injection, persistence configuration, queries, and framework descriptors. Small mistakes in any of these pieces can prevent successful deployment.

Figure: Spring → Jakarta Migration Example

Framework migration requires translating framework semantics, not just source code.

ScarfBench provides a systematic way to evaluate AI agents on enterprise Java framework migration tasks.

This provides a much more realistic measure of modernization quality.

ScarfBench includes both focused migration tasks and whole-application migrations.

Starting from a JSR-based enterprise Java taxonomy, expert migrations create verified implementations across Spring, Jakarta EE, and Quarkus.

We evaluated several state-of-the-art coding agents on ScarfBench.

Despite strong performance on traditional software engineering benchmarks, framework migration remains difficult. Success rates vary considerably across framework pairs and whole-application migrations remain particularly challenging.

Figure: Compile → Deploy → Test Progression

Compile success consistently exceeds deploy success, which in turn exceeds behavioral success. Build success alone significantly overestimates migration quality.

Figure: Migration Outcomes by Target Framework

Migration difficulty depends strongly on the target framework, with Jakarta EE proving particularly challenging.

Beyond measuring success rates, ScarfBench helps us understand how agents behave during modernization.

A migrated application is only useful if it actually builds and runs.

We therefore compared agent-reported outcomes against independent build verification.

Claude Code reported successful builds for 29 out of 30 whole applications.

Only 22 of those applications actually built successfully.

Meanwhile, the single application classified as failed by the agent ultimately built correctly.

This suggests that agent self-assessment should not be treated as a reliable signal of migration completion.

Independent build and test validation remains essential.

Framework migrations rarely affect a single file or layer.

Changes in configuration, services, databases, and web components often cascade across the application.

This suggests that migration is an iterative dependency-resolution process rather than a simple source-to-source transformation.

We used layer revisit frequency as a proxy for migration effort. Layers that required repeated visits typically involved debugging, dependency resolution, or framework adaptation.

Rather than proceeding linearly, agents repeatedly returned to configuration-related artifacts while resolving framework differences and dependency issues.

Not every migration issue originates from source code.

Agents frequently struggled with environmental issues, including:

These operational concerns often delayed validation even when the source-code migration itself was largely complete.

Modernization failures span build systems, deployment environments, dependency injection, databases, endpoints, assertions, and infrastructure.

The biggest challenge in framework modernization is not translating Java code.

It is managing the web of dependencies across configuration, infrastructure, and runtime environments.

While frontier agents can automate substantial portions of the migration process, reliable validation and architectural reasoning remain critical for achieving successful outcomes.

ScarfBench helps expose these challenges and provides a standardized way to measure progress toward truly autonomous application modernization.

ScarfBench is designed as an open resource for researchers and practitioners.

Researchers can compare agent architectures and techniques. Practitioners can use ScarfBench to evaluate modernization solutions before deploying them in production environments.

https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ScarfBench

https://huggingface.co/spaces/ibm-research/ScarfBench

Framework migration remains one of the largest unsolved problems in AI-assisted software engineering. We hope ScarfBench helps the community measure progress and accelerate the next generation of AI-assisted application modernization.

We invite researchers, practitioners, and framework communities to evaluate their agents, contribute new migration scenarios and help advance the state of the art.

#9903. Apple turns iCloud into spy cloud, will start looking at public share links

Content shared with anyone who has the URL will be scanned for 'harmful content,' though the iMaker hasn't defined that term

If you share content using public iCloud links, Apple could soon be looking over your shoulder and checking for "harmful content." The iBiz announced plans to moderate publicly accessible iCloud share links in version 27.3 of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS on a support page published on Tuesday. To clarify, this applies only to iCloud content shared via links created to be accessible to anyone, as opposed to content shared directly with other people.

“Items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content,” Apple explained on the new help page without bothering to define what harmful content means. Based on the wording, it appears those checks will apply to all iCloud items shared using "Anyone with the Link," which Apple says it can also access. The company hasn't explained how the checks will work.

The share-with-anyone option removes end-to-end encryption from the shared item, Apple said, even if Advanced Data Protection, Apple's optional end-to-end encryption feature for supported iCloud data, remains enabled for the account.

“If you try to upload harmful content, Apple reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time,” the help page continues, adding that the iMaker may also block or disable accounts associated with harmful content.

The company also said it reserves the right to involve law enforcement when necessary, suggesting that its undefined "harmful content" category could include child sexual abuse material (CSAM), malware, and other potentially unlawful content.

Without a proper definition of what it defines as harmful, however, iCloud users are essentially left at Apple’s mercy: If it chooses to continue to bend the knee to the Trump administration, for example, content deemed objectionable by the standards of political figures could end up wiped out.

Apple also hasn't explained whether human moderators, automated systems, or both will be responsible for identifying and removing so-called harmful content, or whether any decisions will be left to AI, which can easily be fooled into making a bad moderation call.

The scanning of such content, as mentioned above, begins with version 27.3 of Apple’s various OSes, which were released to developers in beta on Tuesday, with a general release expected in December.

Apple didn’t respond to questions for this story. ®

#9902. Hugging Face and Cerebras bring Gemma 4 to real-time voice AI

For voice AI, latency is a critical parameter. Developers have made tremendous progress in model quality, but the user experience is still often limited by response times. Hugging Face and Cerebras are changing that experience. Today, we demonstrate what becomes possible when an open, modular voice AI architecture is paired with industry-leading inference speed.

The result is a speech-to-speech experience that feels dramatically more natural. Instead of waiting for an AI to respond, conversations flow with the responsiveness users expect from human interaction.

The demo is built as a real-time speech-to-speech pipeline. Each part of the system is modular, open, and replaceable, making it easy for developers to adapt the stack for different assistants, robots, products, or research projects.

This creates a fully open speech-to-speech loop:

The architecture brings together the strength of the open-source AI ecosystem: Cerebras for fast inference, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4 31B for the language model, and Qwen for text-to-speech. Every layer can be inspected, modified, and extended by the developers

Today, some production systems see a reasonable median latency while still experiencing frustrating multi-second delays at the P95. Those delays become even more noticeable when tool calls or multimodal steps require multiple turns.

Cerebras helps solve one of the most important bottlenecks in the stack: the language-model response time. By making inference dramatically faster and more stable, Cerebras allows the rest of the Hugging Face pipeline to shine.

That stability is especially important at the long tail. Many systems can deliver acceptable median response times, but occasional slow responses still make conversations feel unreliable.

This same Hugging Face speech-to-speech pipeline already powers Reachy Mini robots, with more than 9,000 robots in the wild. For robots, voice assistants, and embodied AI, responsiveness is not a cosmetic improvement. It is what makes the interaction feel alive.

The motivation to use Cerebras is therefore not simply cost reduction. It is low latency, predictable performance, and the ability to create real-time experiences that feel natural at scale.

This collaboration reflects a shared belief that the future of AI will be both open and performant. Open-source models, open infrastructure, and breakthrough inference speed together create a foundation for the next generation of conversational AI.

We invite developers to explore the demo, experiment with the code, and help shape what comes next for real-time voice AI.

We even crossed 10k Reachy Minis in the wild 😄

It's exciting to see how Hugging Face and Cerebras are pushing real-time voice technology forward. Fast responses make conversations feel much more comfortable and engaging, and that's exactly what users have been hoping for. 😊 When the delay is reduced, interactions become smoother and more natural, making voice experiences feel less like talking to software and more like having a real conversation.

What I appreciate most is the focus on an open and modular approach. That gives developers more flexibility to build solutions that fit different needs instead of being locked into a single ecosystem. The combination of strong model quality with impressive inference speed could help unlock many practical applications across education, customer support, accessibility, and beyond. 🚀

The emphasis on latency is absolutely the right direction because speed directly shapes the overall experience. Even the smartest system can feel frustrating if every response takes too long. Bringing that waiting time down creates a much more fluid interaction, and it's great to see innovation focused on something users notice immediately. 👏

Looking forward to seeing how this evolves over the coming months... Faster conversations... Better responsiveness... More natural interactions... Exciting progress for developers and users alike... 🌟🙂

#9899. Observations from Running stealmybitcoin.com

Last week, I saw an article on the front page of the New York Times website reporting that a critical vulnerability in PHP had been found. The article, and others like it, claimed any attacker could achieve arbitrary remote code execution on any of the millions of running PHP services worldwide simply by sending a few unauthenticated web requests that exploited the PHP2Shell vulnerability.

My office Slack was buzzing, as were several of my Signal chats with colleagues and friends across the security community.

Rumors swirled about how in-the-wild exploitation caused one tech company to break embargo and leak news of the vulnerability hours before the rest of the community could coordinate disclosure. That hackers were already hacking websites, in the wild, with this exploit and that every hour mattered to get the patches rolled out across 70% of the internet.

Was PHP2Shell the hallmark of a new era whereby uplifted randos could hack any website with a few well-crafted prompts to an AI model?

I looked out my window, expecting perhaps to see the dull apocalyptic glow of fires on the horizon as society collapsed in real time. Nothing.

While online articles and tweets made the rounds about the eleven alarm cyberapocalypse upon us, I struggled to find any reference to a specific website that had been hacked.

Over the following days, a few iconoclasts had pointed out that the vulnerability was rather fiddly in practice (Elias Taylor; Lucas Luitjes) and that hacker groups, while initially quite excited by the exploit’s potential, had started to view it as impractical or difficult (KELA).

Yet at the same time, the national and international press continued to cover a herculean emergency effort to hunt down and patch PHP-based websites across the internet.

Rather than wait around and wonder, I decided to try to figure things out for myself. I had two fundamental questions:

Directly, the answers to the questions are:

Yes. Absolutely. The challenge winner, who has posted a writeup, exploited my server directly over an open internet connection and did so using the PHP2Shell vulnerability (e.g. he did not exploit some other vulnerability in my setup). He did this through a specially crafted exploit which targeted the specific configuration of my PHP installation and the ways in which it was set up on the server.

Not yet. Of tens of thousands of people who attempted the exploit - including in a 9 hour period when the challenge was active after the first successful solve (more on that below…) - only two managed to trigger the print-flag binary and only one, the winner of the challenge, managed to do so in such a way as to extract useful content from the application.

The core idea was pretty simple. I’d rent a cheap VPS for a few weeks, slap a PHP website on it along with the key to a bitcoin wallet, and then wait and see if anyone managed to drain the wallet. Miraculously, the domain name “stealmybitcoin.com” was available, so I took this as a sign from the fates themselves that this experiment had the mandate of heaven.

I slapped $500 of bitcoin into a clean wallet, rented a $2.50/month Debian VPS from a web hosting provider, and told Codex to make me a basic webpage and stick it on the internet with PHP. I configured the server such that a single executable binary print-flag had permissions to read a flag file containing the WIF, took down my firewall, and posted the link to Hacker News to see if anyone would give the challenge a shot.

Things got a little crazy from there. Within the first hour of posting, the link had climbed to the front page of Hacker News (where it stayed for essentially an entire day) and my $2.50/month VPS was under so much load I couldn’t maintain an SSH session.

I eventually scaled my VPS up from 1 vCPU, 500 MB RAM and 10GB of disk space all the way to 2 vCPU, 4096 MB RAM, and 80 GB of SSD. Over the course of the challenge my VPS host temporarily took my site down once because they suspected it was subject to a Distributed Denial of Service attack and once because “we have determined your CPU resource utilization profile is excessive.”

Additionally, due to the nature of the exploit, people were pretty continuously taking down individual PHP workers from high request load, partially successful memory exploitation attempts, and general shenanigans.

Eventually I managed to get things into a relatively steady state (e.g. most people could connect to the website most of the time), with regular resets and health checks standing in for true high-availability hosting. Once the link dropped off the front page of Hacker News, traffic quieted down quite a bit as well.

Due to flaky monitoring, it’s hard to get representative statistics regarding visitor count and traffic patterns. I had set up some pretty reliable logging so I could know if/when the print-flag binary was called and some best-effort logging of web request headers and payloads so I could hopefully understand what happened around that time; for the first few hours of virality, I was blowing through my logrotate configuration (for ~80MB of storage) roughly every 4 minutes thanks to the attention on the site.

As a result, logs of certain PHP crashes and activity around the print-flag file were essentially complete over the duration of the challenge. Broader web request logging only covered 600-ish of the challenge’s 1,600-ish minute duration.

During the 10 hours when I had reliable web request logging:

There’s no statistically credible way to extrapolate over the missing netflow data, but I can confidently say that tens of thousands of players attempted to steal my bitcoin.

I had much more reliable logs of PHP server errors and print-flag executions since they were not rotated under heavy load and were relatively low volume. In these logs, over 26-ish hours, I observed:

My original expectation is that this would be a low traffic honeypot. A few people would poke at it on Hacker News and then it would eventually get snagged by some botnet/scanner/automated exploitation tool that would steal my bitcoin. I’d write a little blog post about the logs from the hour or so around the exploit and then move on.

I didn’t remotely expect it to go viral in the way that it did. The virality was nice - it brought a lot of eyes on the challenge, got me a quick answer to my research question, and some people even chipped in and increased the size of the bitcoin prize wallet.

The virality was also rough in that suddenly many actual PHP security experts (and many non-experts too) had opinions about me, my motivations, and my web administration skills!

The first critique was that the server was unexploitable. Some claimed that it was literally just an nginx page (e.g. no PHP at all), while others claimed that the specific configuration of the server made it impossible to exploit.

I’m still not 100% sure how correct these claims were, as some people were causing SIGSEGVs to throw on the original version of the challenge.

However, I did make several modifications to the website that I felt were fair adjustments to increase the feasibility of the challenge without just deliberately making the server vulnerable.

First, I added a php-version.php page, which was served alongside the already PHP-hosted index.html page, in case the active participation of the PHP interpreter was necessary for the exploit. While some of the early reporting on PHP2Shell suggested this maybe wasn’t a strict requirement of exploitation (e.g. https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce : “Exploitation does not depend on a flaw in the application’s code: even a simple “Hello World” application running on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.”), it seems plausible to me that the part of the PHP SAPI server that serves .html files could be immune to these tasks.

I also added a ping.php page that responds with the word pong whenever someone POSTS the value ping to the server. This very simple application was added in case exploitation required PHP to dynamically react to user-supplied input. To me these two requirements (reacts to user-supplied input, runs .php pages) are pretty universal across real-world applications, so adding support for these code paths did not undermine the spirit of the challenge.

There was some other feedback, which I largely ignored, requesting specific variants of the PHP applications, or modifications to the (very basic) nginx proxy configuration I put in front of the website to help with routing, challenge isolation, and logging. It’s possible that if I made further modifications in this vein, more people would’ve been able to solve the challenge. There is no specific evidence to prove that this would be the case.

The second major hosting issue I had is more easily expressed by a video. This is how I exported the WIF private key for my bitcoin wallet that I used in the challenge (Note: the wallet shown here is a different empty wallet. Please don’t use this key since I’ve recorded a video of it online!):

I thought I was putting the key to the wallet in the challenge based on this flow. Turns out I wasn’t. The WIF I exported turned out to be a parent key in a derivation path for the wallet address holding the bitcoin. I’m still not entirely sure which combination of credentials I should’ve provided to make the bitcoin stealable. If I run future challenges of this nature, I’ll probably make the flag the full wallet recovery key instead of any individual private key.

So the winner got the real bitcoin key from the server, but couldn’t use it to move any of the money in the branch wallet derived from that parent key.

Luckily, they reached out over email and provided exceptionally detailed proof including: the full text of the wallet key on the server, its hash, the exact timestamp when they exploited the server, the exact IP address they used to exploit the server, the exact payload they used to exploit the server, AI chat turns from when they developed the exploit, and a full writeup of the exploit they used.

With this information I was able to pull up the full trace in my logs, match down to the second the exploitation time with my logs on the print-flag binary and confirm that they did in fact know the full value of the flag file on the server.

Congrats to the winner for not only solving the challenge, but also solving the secret hidden challenge of keeping excellent exploit logs!

So what did I learn from this experience?

I launched the website out of a degree of skepticism around the breathless reporting of a serious PHP CVE despite a dearth of real-world victims of this attack.

To be honest, I think that was a bad take on my part. PHP2Shell is the real deal. It’s an exploitable vulnerability and a sufficiently motivated adversary, with the help of AI, can absolutely use it to hack a website even when they do not have direct access to memory addresses or the physical server to tailor their exploitation pathway.

If you are running a PHP-based website today, you should absolutely patch PHP2Shell.

I fully expect over the coming months we will see more and more working general purpose exploit chains for PHP2Shell.

If you operate a service that is sufficiently valuable or public enough to warrant specialized attention, my experience with stealmybitcoin.com makes me believe it is a matter of when, not if, someone could target a working PHP2Shell exploit specifically to your system configuration.

On the flip side, I believe stealmybitcoin.com tells us a lot about the current state of AI-assisted cyber exploitation. Out of tens of thousands of people attempting to hack a website with a publicly known (and exploitable!) CVE on it, only two managed to get close to triggering the vulnerability.

While some of the server-side changes I made to make exploitation easier may have had an impact (e.g. the winner solved the challenge about 3 hours after I added php-version.php to the server), many thousands of hackers were unable to trigger the flag binary over the 9-ish hours between the winner’s successful solve and the time when I took the challenge offline.

It’s pretty clear that we aren’t at a time, yet, where an inexpert attacker can take a top LLM + a difficult CVE (like PHP2Shell was) and turn it into a reliable cyber-attack tool.

It does seem that we’re drawing closer to that point every day though. I don’t think there’s any good way to stuff this cat back into the bag, but I do hope that hard work over the coming months across the open source and systems security ecosystem will make it so that hard exploits remain hard.

As someone who has spent a good chunk of my career doing offensive security research, PHP2Shell seems like another example of why enabling good people to find bugs quickly and publicly, so that everyone can get a jump on patching them, is as important as it has ever been.

My interests include cybersecurity, space, software engineering, and policy.
